utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Good day to all. Case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to greet everyone present: Members of the Prosecution, Defence counsel, the accused, and I wouldn't want to forget to mention everyone else in the courtroom. We'll be continuing with our hearing today on Monday, the 10th of July, 2006, and we have a witness who will soon be called, but first I'd like to tell you something about the admission of documents pending in the case of the witness Manolic and in the case of -- in this case we still haven't ruled, the Chamber hasn't ruled, so before the witness is called into the courtroom, I give the floor to the Defence and the Prosecution so that they can mention the numbers of the documents that they would like to be admitted into evidence. Mr. Kovacic sent a number of letters this weekend. That's the second issue I'd like to deal with. So Mr. Kovacic, I will give you the floor now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I really hate taking up time before a witness is called into the courtroom. However, since you have seen copies of the correspondence between myself and the Prosecution - and I read my letters in collaboration with my colleagues - given that you have seen copies of this correspondence, I will try to be brief. We believe that the Prosecution is yet again acting in a way that is preventing the Defence from preparing in an adequate way for its cross-examination. We have also made this objection with regard to (Redacted), Manolic, Tomislav [as interpreted] and other witnesses. In this particular case the Prosecution informs us of the documents that they intend to use with this witness, and they also inform us of the subject of his evidence, but this is contrary to your decision dated the 30th of November, and it's also contrary to the written -- the oral instructions of the Chamber dated the 3rd of July. That was a discussion held before the witness Manolic was heard. There was a similar objection that was made. The Prosecution has provided information about documents it intends to use through witnesses and about the subject of the testimony in a manner that is not sufficiently transparent, in our opinion. For example, the witness statement, statement given by a witness to investigators of the Prosecution on the 20th of January, this statement was disclosed to us in good time. This statement is quite different from the kind of statements we usually receive. It's difficult to provide you with a precise definition, but in fact it's a sort of summary. It's not the usual type of statement we receive. The language used is almost the kind of language you use in a telegram. And then we have another problem with regard to agreements on events up to April, 1992. Then up until May, 1992, we have no other information. So the Defence can assume on the basis of that statement that the witness won't be examined about the period from April, 1992, to May, 1992, nor will there be any documents from that period of time, because it's quite obvious that during that period of time the witness was somewhere that is not relevant to our case. With that statement dated the 20th of January, 2004, we were also provided with a list of documents, 11 documents, that the witness provided to the Prosecution, but the statement doesn't show that these documents were discussed. We know nothing about the character of these documents or of the objective or the link to the witness's statement. This is important because that could provide us with information that we need for our cross-examination. And then, before this testimony, we received a proofing chart in good time and other documents mentioned that the Prosecution intends to use, and this list is not identical to the list that was provided as an attachment to the witness's statement. Together with the proofing chart, certain documents were listed which were compiled from April to May, 1993, and this is a period that the witness hadn't provided any previous statements with regard to that period. The Prosecution also didn't mention anything about the link between these statements and the witness, nor were we informed of how one could establish whether the witness was involved in the events covered by the documents. We don't know whether he had seen the documents, whether he participated in the compiling of the documents, whether they were addressed to him, whether these documents were addressed to the witness or did the witness simply collect these documents at someone's request, or perhaps on his own initiative when he responded to the request made by the Prosecution for testimony. Today, in the morning, the Prosecution provided us with more information about the expected testimony of the witness and, according to the information provided for today, he mentions the paragraphs in the indictment that are not quite identical to what was mentioned in the proofing chart previously provided, and then there are also certain allegations that are contained in the statement the witness made in January, 2004, on the 20th of January, 2004. So it mentions meetings with General Praljak, and in the information we were provided with, these meetings took place during a period of time that the witness doesn't refer to in his previous statement. Then there are new allegations about the Patriotic League. The witness didn't mention anything about this on the 20th of January, 2004. Then there are certain claims about an event on the 20th of June, 1992. Similarly, this wasn't previously addressed by the witness. And finally, there are certain claims about changes made to the public telephone network, and similarly, in the first statement this is not mentioned. So it was only this morning that we found out that these events, these facts might be subjects with regard to which the witness would testify. I have informed the Prosecution about the problems we encountered as soon as we established the existence of such problems. That took place on Saturday. This morning the Prosecution replied to the letter. You have received a copy of the letter. I'm not going to talk above my colleagues, but the Prosecution claims that they're not acting contrary to the rules or to common practice. They also claim that they have disclosed everything in good faith and in good time to the Defence. In conclusion, acting in such a way makes it impossible for the Defence to prepare adequately for its cross-examination, or at least makes it significantly more difficult for the Defence, and acting in such a way is contrary to the instructions issued by the Chamber on the 3rd of November and the 3rd of July, as I've already said. And finally, acting in this manner is contrary to the principle of a fair trial because, I have already said, it's impossible for the Defence to prepare adequately, and I therefore suggest that we postpone the testimony of this witness. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, may it please the Court, Mr. Kovacic appears to have certain -- a certain model that he would like all ICTY witness statements to comply with. There is no such model. I do not write these statements. I do not take these statements. They are taken by investigators, sometimes over a period of years, and I may see those statements for the first time a short time before coming into court. The statement that was disclosed to the Defence is exactly the statement that was taken. Now, if Mr. Kovacic had been -- had taken the statement, perhaps he would have taken the statement differently. I can only disclose what I have to disclose, and what I have disclosed is the statement that was taken in January, 2004. It's not a summary. It's a statement. And Mr. Kovacic knows full well that it looks very similar to hundreds of other similar statements that he has seen, that he and I have both seen over the past seven or eight years. So that's just not -- his characterisation and attacks on the statement are just not fair. The documents that were disclosed, Your Honour, include both the documents that were attached to his statement, which the Defence have had for some months. I emphasise the word "months." They've had those statements -- or documents attached to his statement which were disclosed according to the Rules. Various exhibits or documents were then listed in the proofing sheet -- well, number one, first of all they were listed in the 65 ter exhibit list that was filed in January. So they've been on the witness -- on the exhibit list since January. Beyond that, they have been connected -- specifically connected to this witness through his proofing chart. So they were disclosed with the original witness statement some months and months ago, they were disclosed again in our 65 ter filing in January this year; three, they were disclosed and listed again in the proofing chart that was provided to the Defence. Now, I respectfully submit that's ample notice to the Defence of the exhibits and documents that we intend to use with this witness and/or which indicate the fair scope of his questioning and examination. As counsel indicated, members of the Prosecution met with Mr. Cupina yesterday, and -- and as a result -- and that was the first time anyone from the OTP has had any substantive contact or conversation with Mr. Cupina since January of 2004. In the course of that discussion with him, some additional things were said which, out of fairness, we believed should in fact be additionally disclosed to the Defence and they were disclosed as soon as possible this morning. The meeting went into -- as I understand it, went into the meeting -- went into the evening last night, a summary statement was prepared, and it was disclosed to the Defence this morning. Sorry, I'm being signalled by Judge Prandler to slow down. My apology. I don't know what more we could have done, Your Honour, to get that information to the Defence than what's been done. As I said in the letters, Your Honour, and -- well, as I said in the letters, I think it's very unfortunate that we have to get into a practice of exchanging these kinds of letters. Up until this letter, I had intentionally refrained from engaging in this -- such an exchange, and the record will show, if anyone wants to go through the correspondence over the past number of months, will show the number of Defence letters that I simply chose not to respond to, to avoid exactly this sort of tit for tat back and forth and hoped that it would eventually go away. But it now appears that this has become standard practice, I won't say for other Defence but certainly for Mr. Kovacic, and therefore I have no choice now except to respond to such letters in kind so that the record is clear and so that when your court officers and staff see these letters, don't assume that they -- or understand that they are accurate or that they represent the full picture and therefore it's necessary for the Prosecution to respond with its -- at least its view of events. So that's what we've tried to do. Your Honour, I believe there's been complete and fair disclosure concerning this witness and that we are prepared to go forward to offer his evidence today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Kovacic, I have read your letters with interest, as well as Mr. Scott's response. Do sit down. I'll give you the floor when I'm finished. It seems that you are not aware of how investigations are carried out before this Tribunal. Initially, the investigators go to receive statements given by witnesses who might be able to enlighten the Tribunal with regard to events that took place. As you, Mr. Scott, have said, it was on the 20th of January, 2004, that the witness who will be called into courtroom today was heard, and that's when he gave a statement. There were certain attachments to his statement, and these attachments were discussed when the investigator and the witness met. Once this statement had been given, as in the case of other statements, this was provided to the Confirming Judge, and I can inform you of the fact that I was the Confirming Judge. An indictment is confirmed with regard to statements taken. Once the confirmation has been made, the Prosecutor continues to carry out his investigations, and when a witness is heard, in this case in 2004, there are certain other -- there is certain other information that crops up. Pursuant to 65 ter, Rule 65 ter, the Prosecution has to provide a summary about the subject of the examination-in-chief, but it's a summary. It's not for the Prosecution -- or it's not necessary for the Prosecution to mention all the areas that the witness will be questioned about. It's a summary, and this summary will also refer to the written statement. So the Prosecution has the right to ask questions on the basis of the written statement, but he also has the right to ask the witness questions about -- about the charges in the indictment that are referred to in the summary. In the summary, it says violations 1, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 19, 20, 21, 24, 25 and 26. And the Prosecution said this concerned paragraphs 5, 13, 14, 17, 39, 96, 97, 100, 112, 114, 116, 122, 131. In addition, when I read through the sheet of paper that you have seen as well, the accused have been mentioned in a certain order with regard to the questions that will be put. Mr. Pusic is in the first place, then there's Mr. Stojic, third place Mr. Praljak, in fourth place Petkovic, and then Coric and Prlic. So this chart quite clearly shows that the accused who is mostly concerned is Mr. Pusic, then Mr. Stojic, and then Mr. Praljak. This is common practice before this Tribunal, and on a number of occasions you have made submissions stating that the Prosecution doesn't have the right to put certain questions. It has the right to put questions on the basis of the summary that we have here, on the basis of the paragraphs referred to, and also on the basis of what is of interest in the indictment. What do the Rules say? According to the Rules, everything is quite clear. We're interested in Rule 89 and Rule 90. According to 89, the Chamber applies the Rules mentioned in section 3: "A Chamber shall apply the rules of evidence set forth in this Section," and is not "bound by national rules of evidence," Croatian rules of evidence, French rules of evidence, American rules of evidence. This is quite secondary. So that's what is stated in the Rules. It says the Chamber "shall apply the rules of evidence which will best favour a fair determination of the matter before it and are consonant with the spirit of the Statute and the general principles of laws" in cases not otherwise provided for in this section. And paragraph (C) says the Chamber "may admit any relevant evidence which it deems to have probative value." So this is how one proceeds when hearing witnesses. Each time a witness appears, we don't want to find ourselves in a situation where we have to deal with exchanges of correspondence. Things will be a lot clearer as of the 4th of September, because by that time the Prosecution will have provided us with a complete list of witnesses and documents together with the relevant paragraphs. So there will be no surprises once this has been done. But I must note that this witness statement is one that was provided to you a long time ago, and therefore you are in a position to conduct your cross-examination and deal with any problems that you might encounter in the course of your cross-examination. So this is the problem that we are facing, and it's one that I fail to understand. Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I fully agree with your position, with your explanation, and I adhere by your -- the principles you have mentioned, except in certain cases, but with regard to disclosing the subject of the examination, with regard to the information provided in the first 65 ter chart, well, all that is correct. However, the Prosecution is providing us with different types of information. Here they're mentioning -- here we're mentioning the fact that there's a conflict of information. We received one type of information in January, we received other information later on, another type of information in the witness's statement. So the Prosecution is saying something that I didn't say. We received all this material a long time ago. There's no problem as far as that is concerned, but I cannot be provided with a statement and all these other charts if on each occasion I'm provided with conflicting information. There's one period, April, 1992, May, 1993, and this hasn't been covered. So my main argument, and that's the purpose of Rule 89, and Rule 90. My argument is that things should be transparent, and as the situation is, the situation is not completely transparent because each new document, each new list confuses us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may be of assistance. I think what -- I can understand Mr. Scott's position. He's not out in the field. An investigator is sent out to -- to meet with the witness. That investigator is not necessarily a jurist, doesn't have a law degree, certainly is not a Judge or not an investigative Judge. What we see here - and this is a perfect example - is where certain information was provided to the investigator and at some point during the meeting the gentleman provided the investigator with certain documents. We don't see any discussion with respect to those particular documents that were handed over, which begs the question if an investigator is out there to collect information and somebody comes with a bunch of documents, why wouldn't the investigator ask questions? It just perhaps highlights the fact that we're not dealing with trained investigators as one would find in the continental system, and perhaps that's why we're at somewhat of a disadvantage, because now we're being asked -- we're trying to figure out how could this witness possibly discuss these documents when he didn't discuss them with the Prosecutor or the Prosecution's representative in the field. And when you look at the documents that we're presented, he hasn't generated those documents, and that -- and that -- and so that poses a problem for us: How do we prepare for such a witness? And I think that's what Mr. Kovacic was trying to -- to relay to Mr. Scott. And I don't know if that's of any help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Karnavas. You've dealt with the problem in a very clear way. You have presented it in a very clear way. It's true that when a witness statement is taken he mentions an entire series of events, and certain documents are attached to the statement. I don't know how American investigators or British or Australian investigators proceed, but a French investigator would have said, "We're presenting you with Attachment A which relates to the 21st of May and 21st of June, 1993. It's been signed by Mr. Pavlovic. What do you have to say about this?" And then in the written statement it would say, "The witness stated the following ..." and then he'd comment on each document. That's how one would proceed. Unfortunately, in the case of the work carried out by investigators from this Tribunal, we can see that we have lists of documents that appear, but the witness concerned doesn't make any comments on these documents to the investigator. And today we will be presenting the witness with documents, but the witness didn't make any statements with regard to these documents when he made his written statement. So this is the actual problem. But it's been partially solved because the proceedings are adversarial and, as a result, the witness will mention what his -- the position is, and you'll be able to cross-examine the witness with regard to his statements. Ideally, however, the witness would have already commented on the documents attached to his written statements. Unfortunately, this was not done. So I do agree with you as far as this issue is concerned. Mr. Scott, as we have now managed to identify the problem, you'll be able to clarify the situation for us too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Two points, Your Honour. In looking at the statement, first of all, one of the comments, one of the complaints that's been raised is that the -- there's not been adequate notice that events related -- concerning 1992, excuse me, were -- would be covered by this witness, and I just this moment ago -- it really didn't take more than a few minutes, I just now went back through the statement very quickly and there are a number of references throughout the document that talk about events in 1992: Paragraph 7, paragraph 8, paragraph -- excuse me, paragraph 17, paragraph 19. It's just simply not accurate -- paragraph 35. It's simply not accurate to say the document gives no indication of addressing events earlier than 1993, and the statement -- that's just not at all what the statement says. Secondly, Your Honour, in terms of the documents and in defence of my investigative colleagues, this was a situation, and this is a situation that happens not infrequently, and again Mr. Kovacic is well aware of this from his work with this Tribunal since 1998 when he and I worked together on the Kordic/Cerkez case on opposite sides again. He knows full well that what frequently happens in this situation and what happens here is that when a witness is met in the field, documents are presented to the investigator which neither the investigator nor the interpreter nor anyone has seen for the first time. And anyone who has a copy of Mr. Cupina's statement, paragraph 38, it says the following: "Below is the list of documents that I have turned over to the investigator from the Tribunal," and then it lists annexes A through annex K. Now, as I said in my letter, Your Honour, this happens in the field. Now, I don't know exactly what the schedule was. I don't know exactly what the circumstance was when the -- this investigative team met with this witness. They may have had a limited time. They may have had reasons they had to be back in Sarajevo later that night. There could be a jillion different reasons. They show up for a witness, they may have allocated a couple of hours to see the witness, they meet that witness, and the witness for the first time handles them -- hands them a bundle of documents, untranslated, all in B/C/S. Now, at that particular moment the investigators may not have any opportunity or time sufficient time or preparation to take the -- take the witness through those documents in any sort of prepared way. So it's not a situation where the investigators prepare the interview in The Hague, took with them certain documents to ask the witness about, which of course would have been prepared ahead of time, and proceeded in such a fashion. This was a situation quite the opposite. This is a situation in which the witness himself unexpectedly provided the investigative team with a number of documents in the field on the spot, and only -- only certain things could be done to deal with the documents, if at all, at that particular moment. So that is the situation. I don't think that, in my respectful submission, in this respect I don't think American or British or French investigators work that much different than others. I think it's unfair. I think it's unfair to suggest that one system's investigators are superior to the others. I have worked with some very fine -- I've worked with some of the best investigators in the world in the United States. I've also worked with some of the poorest investigators in the world in the United States, and I think that's true in every system in the world, including all those represented on the Bench. So I think it's an unfair statement by counsel to attack the statement in this way. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Murphy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for the sake of completeness, I think we should note that it was only last week that the Trial Chamber rendered an oral decision regarding the disclosure of new information to the Defence in a case in which the Prosecution, at a late date during a proofing session, for example, became aware of certain information that had not previously been disclosed. That was on the 3rd of July. The transcript reference begins at page 4249, I believe. Your Honour, if the Trial Chamber will recall, there was some very explicit guidance given to the parties at that time, part of which was that when such information comes to the attention of the Prosecution, it should be made instantly available to the Defence by e-mail, telephone, or fax, contacting the Defence so that they should be in a position to prepare a cross-examination. There was also more general guidance given as to the -- the -- the general period of two weeks prior to the testimony of a witness, during which disclosure of the relevant documents should be made. And, Your Honour, just for consistency, I think we should not conclude the discussion without at least referring to that decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, it is true that we gave that ruling on the 3rd of July, and I have it before me, and it referred to new points which did not come up during the written statement or testimony. Then it is up to the Prosecution to inform the Defence within a deadline. Now, with respect to the 20th of January, 2004, statement, were there any new points that you would like to ask the witness about, examine him on? And if that is the case, when did you inform the Defence thereof?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: There are points, Your Honour, that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: There were points, Your Honour, that were added, that were amplified on by the witness which we felt should be additionally disclosed. All -- many of these points -- sorry, not all. I don't want to overstate. Many of these points were covered in the documentation that was attached to his statement and in the exhibits that were identified by the Prosecution previously. So I'm not going to say that is that most of these things, they were entirely new, but he indeed said some things that we thought should be disclosed. Now, this -- the preparation of this witness was completed at -- shortly before 10.00 p.m. last night, and the additional disclosure was made this morning. So I'm not sure how much faster the Prosecution can turn around that information. If it receives that information sometime on Sunday day evening and turns it over on Monday morning, I'm not sure, Your Honour, how we're supposed to do any better than that. As in terms of the previous guidelines given by the Chamber last week, the Chamber may recall that Mr. Cupina was a fill-in witness, if you will, when other witnesses would not -- were not available, and had already been scheduled previous to the guidelines given last week, and of course we couldn't possibly comply with all -- strictly comply with all guidelines last week. Unfortunately, I have not yet developed any sort of a time machine that allows me to go back in time to do such things. However, we wanted to use the time wisely and use the time this week. Mr. Cupina was disclosed some days ago, and is indeed prepared to testify to use the available court time. I should say to balance this presentation, Your Honour, as the Court knows from last week, there was also another witness scheduled for later this week, and because indeed it turned out to have been some problems with the disclosure - some of the CDs didn't work, some of them -- there were other problems with the CDs and translations - we indeed, I think -- I hope Defence counsel will confirm, postponed that witness out of -- out of -- out of those concerns, based on those concerns. So I think the Prosecution has acted in good faith on both counts. We have done everything we can to prepare this witness and present as much information to the Defence as possible. It probably isn't perfect, perhaps we'll never be able to meet up -- to live up to Mr. Kovacic's standards, but we're doing the best that we can. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Judges would like to have the witness shown in. Would Madam Usher bring him in, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And while we're getting the witness, Your Honour, we do have to deal with the issue of exhibits from the previous witness, if we could do that at some point. I just -- as a reminder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I haven't forgotten that. In principle, we'll do that tomorrow when we get through this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. First of all, I'd like to check to see if you can hear properly in your own language. If you can, tell me that you can hear and understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear you and I can understand you as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could you give me your first and last name and date of birth now, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Suad Cupina. I was born on the 11th of November, 1951, in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what is your profession -- profession or occupation now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am a professional deputy in the Assembly -- or, rather, the cantonal Sarajevo Assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, have you ever testified before an International Tribunal before or a national court on the facts that -- and circumstances that took place in your country in 1992 and 1993 and 1994, or is this the first time that you're testifying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have never testified either before an International Tribunal or a court in Bosnia-Herzegovina. This is the first time that I am testifying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm now going to ask you to read out the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated, Mr. Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw you coming in with a large binder under your arm and I saw all the Defence counsel looking at what you were bringing in, so I'm going to tell you that you're going to have to answer questions without looking at the binder. You can put it down by your feet. You do not have the right to consult those documents. So I hope you've understood that. The documents must be set aside. I'm going to give you some brief information about the proceedings and how they are conducted. You are, first of all, going to be answering questions put to you by the representatives of Madam Carla Del Ponte and those people who you have already met after, as we have heard, yesterday at 10.00, which was very late indeed, but the Prosecution had no means of seeing you before that. Once the Prosecution has completed its examination-in-chief, and I have been told that that will take one and a half hours, dealing with basic issues, you will then be answering questions put to you by the Defence. They are the Defence teams of the six accused, and they are sitting to your left. I don't know the order in which the Defence teams will be asking their questions, but they will be conducting what we call the cross-examination. The four Judges sitting in front of you can also ask you questions at any point in time if they consider that necessary and if they believe your answers could provide additional explanation. If you have any difficulties whatsoever during the examination, please don't hesitate to let us know. Now, for technical reasons we have to make pauses after one and a half hours of sitting, so the next break will be at approximately 3.40. We make 20-minute breaks and reconvene after that. So today we shall be working until 7.00 p.m., and tomorrow we start again at 9.00 and work until 12.30. Then we'll have a lunch break and go on working from 2.00 to 5.15, and I hope by that time we'll have completed your examination and cross-examination and you'll be able to go back home either Tuesday evening or Wednesday morning. So that, in general terms, is how the proceedings are conducted and what you can expect, because you have been called as a Prosecution witness to give testimony with regard to certain facts and circumstances. Having said that, Mr. Scott, without further ado, I give you the floor. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I wonder if there's anything in the binder that the gentleman brought over that was not provided to the Prosecution, which means that it wasn't provided to the Defence. If that is the case -- if that is the case -- and if the gentleman brought that material in order to look at it, I would ask that he make it available to us to copy it. We could do so during the break. It wouldn't be any inconvenience to the gentleman. And I see he's shaking his head, so I assume he brought it for his own personal use and doesn't wish to share it with us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've also observed the witness has in front of him a book which I don't believe will be tendered by the Prosecution but I believe may deal with certain subjects of his testimony and may it be made clear to the witness that that book should also remain closed until referred to, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said a moment ago, keep your documents closed. You will just be answering questions put to you by the Prosecution unless they show you some documents. But since last night, if the Prosecutor provided you with documents that you have there, are those some of the documents that you have beside you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure I understood, Your Honour. I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, these are documents that the witness brought with him personally, they were not provided to him by the Prosecution. I have explained to the witness, on meeting him briefly today, that he would not be able to use those documents in court unless some specific leave was given by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may interject here. Two points: First of all, I'm not suggesting that the Prosecution provided those notes to the gentleman; however, if the gentleman is going to be looking at anything that's in that binder that was not provided to the Prosecution or to the Defence, I would object. I would like to see it in advance. That's number one. Number two, when the gentleman closed his binder, I can see from my vantage point that he has a sheet of paper that's inside the binder but very visible. There you go. He's pulling it out right now. And so -- yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are the instructions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is that piece of paper, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Several instructions for witnesses with respect to interpretation. Nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I have to ask. I have to ask. It looked like --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- to me, so I just needed to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Having settled that point, it is 3.00, Mr. Scott. You can begin your examination-in-chief, and you have 40 minutes before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, just to -- the Judge touched on some of your background but let me touch on it just a bit more. You were born in Mostar, sir, in what year?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: On the 11th of November, 1951.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I understand that you lived there more or less continuously until 1970 when you moved away for a time. You returned to Mostar in approximately 1980, and you have generally lived in Mostar since 1980; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I understand you are a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina, you are of the Islamic faith, and I also understand that your wife is of the Roman Catholic faith; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm going to object to that, to making references to one's spouse as if that is something to be given credit for, for the purposes of credibility. I don't think it's proper under these circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Continue, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I understand that you are a -- or have been quite -- quite talented and skilled in karate and there was a time when in fact you were the European champion in karate; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: Yes. I am the multiple champion of the former Yugoslavia, as a sportsman. I was the team selector for Yugoslavia and of Bosnia-Herzegovina now. And Bosnia-Herzegovina has the best team in the history of sports.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is that an interest that you have in -- in common with Mr. Coric?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Coric was a pupil of mine in karate, and he came to Mostar in 1986 because his father wanted him to come and asked me to help him with respect to university and the machine engineering faculty, and he -- the club, the Dzemal Bijedic -- at the Dzemal Bijedic University was one of the most successful clubs in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I understand you have a bachelor's degree in economics from Mostar and you also have a master's degree in physical culture; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: Yes. I graduated from the high school of economics in Sarajevo, graduated from the faculty in Mostar, and am now -- I have now gained an MA in the sphere of physical culture and I'm on my way to getting a Ph.D.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, I'm not going to go through every detail of your previous occupations and that sort of thing, or education, but in 1986 you began working for a tourist agency in Mostar. Sometime in around 1990 or 1991, were you a member of the reserve police? Did you become a member of the reserve police in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Sorry, I have a little question in between. You are working on a Ph.D. in economics or in physical culture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, sometime in 1990 or 1991, did you become a member of the reserve police in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: On the 19th of September, 1991. I became a reservist of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I was activated into the reserve police force of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which means that on the 19th of September, 1991, upon the arrival of the Serb and Montenegro reservists on the territory of Mostar municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And there did come a time when you became not only that you were essentially mobilised or activated, but did you serve both in the police and did you later serve as a soldier during the war in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I did work within the wartime reserve station with the wartime deployment of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it was called the war police station, which encompassed the area from the entrance of Mostar until -- up until the old bridge or, rather, the right bank of the river Neretva next to the police station in Kamena Zgrada. After that I continued working as a member of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Some of these things, sir, we will come to in a few minutes. In terms your background, is it correct that you wrote a book about some of the events in Bosnia-Herzegovina published in 2006?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: I published the book sometime in January, 2006. The publishing house is the Society of Intellectuals of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I'm the author of the book, and I printed it in Des, which is a firm in Sarajevo, and it is entitled "The Defence and Treachery -- and Traitors Related to Bosnia-Herzegovina." It's part of the truth as I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And does this book cover primarily the period 1991 to 1995?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: That book encompasses that period, and I deal with Serbian Fascism and Tudjman's Fascism, or, rather, the aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina and all the people who took part in breaking up the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, during the 1990s, is it correct, sir, that the -- the media publication Oslobodjenje published a series of articles prepared or written by you focussing on your experiences and the experiences of others during the war in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: In 1993, upon my arrival in Sarajevo with the gentleman from Oslobodjenje or, rather, another paper called Vecernje Novine, I published articles about a series of events that took place in Mostar. It was a series, 16 in Vecernje Novine. It was not only a story told by me but it concerned many of the other people that took part in the happenings of Mostar during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, sir, the last question on your background: Are you currently writing a second book on the war, that is the Balkan war in the -- roughly again the period 1991, 1995?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: As I call the first book Book One, the second and third books are nearing completion, and if I have the financial means, I hope to publish it shortly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, sir, with this background in mind, can I have -- ask for the registry's assistance in showing you Exhibit 1376, P 01376. And once you see that, sir, and if you need the -- to see other pages or want to scroll down or what have you, you just need to ask for the courtroom staff to assist you in looking further at other parts of the document. But if you've seen that document, can you just -- I'm not asking you any questions about the content of the document at the moment, but can you just tell us -- first of all, tell us what this document is and the approximate date of its preparation.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: This document is a sequence of events that took place in Mostar and the surrounding parts already in September, 1992. The Cultural Club of the Muslims compiled an analysis of all the events in the socio-political life of the town of Mostar. In 1993, an analysis of the state administration in the territory of Herzegovina was compiled on how to establish legal power and authority, because the HZ HB toppled the entire state system in Bosnia-Herzegovina in the Mostar area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. If it will assist you, can you look at the last page of the document and tell us the date of its -- that the -- the date of the document. I don't want to say publication necessarily, but the date indicated on the document.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: That document was typed out in February, 1993. The authors of the text are Maslo Sead - he is the current ambassador of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Copenhagen, Denmark - then there was Hamdija Jahic, who is an active duty ambassador today in Sofia, Bulgaria; and Ismet Campara, who lives and works in Mostar. Sead Maslo is married to my sister Merima.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, what were you doing in terms of vocationally or in the military, or what were you doing as of February, 1993, when this document was finalised?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: At that time, in February, 1993, that is, around the 14th of February I went to Sarajevo with a friend of mine, the late Midhat Hujka. That was on the 14th of February, 1993, and I informed the republican authorities about the situation in Mostar, about all the developments and trends in the legal sphere, political sphere, jurisprudence, on a social level and social -- and so on, and brought with me a number of documents which violated the official legal system by the HZ HB, as it was called.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may interject here, Your Honour. Mr. Scott's questions are rather specific. I assume that he has a reason for those questions. I would expect the gentleman, who is rather educated, to answer the questions. It makes it difficult for me to object otherwise, because I'm going to be objecting on the basis of the question, and I don't wish to interfere with the gentleman's narration, but he should stick to answering the questions. Secondly, I wish to point out that the document is dated. We don't know whether this is the exact date. He can read what the date is; it doesn't mean that this was actually created. And I would like some foundation more before we go into this document, or otherwise I will be objecting strenuously as to this document being used through this particular gentleman, because again, as I point out, when the gentleman spoke with the Prosecutors or the representative of the Prosecutor, he did not see fit to show it to them and discuss it with them at the time that he gave his interview. Now, obviously, he can't wait to discuss the document, and this is sort of an ambush.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. So what is the link between that document and the witness, apart from the fact that one of the three authors is his brother-in-law?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I was about to get to that, Your Honour, and the question -- I did put a specific question to the witness, which I'll come back to in a moment. For the most part I don't take any quarrel with -- have any quarrel with Mr. Karnavas's comments, except that again, Your Honour, it's just -- it's completely unfair and inappropriate to say -- when he says -- Mr. Karnavas says on line 10 of page 29: "... he did not see fit to show it to them and discuss it with them at the time that he gave his interview. Now, obviously, he can't wait to discuss the document, and this is sort of an ambush." Your Honour, that is just unfair commentary. For the reasons indicated earlier, there is nothing to suggest that this witness did not see fit to discuss it earlier. That is pure commentary by Mr. Karnavas, and it's inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: There is nothing in the statement that shows that the gentleman tried to speak with them and the OTP didn't want to hear him at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It's really an unfair assumption that you make. There is no reason to make such an assumption. It has been explained that we do not know exactly what happens at the moment when these documents were handed over, so cynical remarks like he did not see it to be fit are not in their place here. Please, Mr. Karnavas, keep fair. You ask fairness of others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. And they have a translator at the time that they're doing the interview. When the gentleman provided those documents, the translator could have looked at them, but there's nothing in -- in his statement at the time where he discussed the documents. Now we're going to hear for the very first time since 2004 what these documents mean to this particular gentleman. It is an ambush to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Scott. The document that has suddenly appeared, would you ask your questions so that we understand how the document appeared and what the document is that you wish to examine him on. Perhaps he knows about the document because of his brother-in-law, but anyway, ask the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All questions were intended to be asked about ten minutes ago, Your Honour, before these interventions. It's not really fair to say that the document suddenly appeared. The document was provided in 2004, not suddenly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Cupina, please listen directly to my question and answer specifically the question that I ask you in this regard, and we'll take this in steps. I asked you, by way of background leading into this matter, can you tell the Judges what you were doing, what activities you were engaged in in approximately February, 1993; January, February, 1993.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: Already on the 6th of June, 1992, I was appointed the commander of the military police of the Mostar region. On the 20th of June, 1992, I was unable to get approval from Mr. Boban for us to form the police jointly, because they insisted on a separate police of their own, that there was no Bosnia and Herzegovina in existence, that they would be making their own state, so that I went underground and informed the state top officials about events in Mostar. Before that, in September, 1992, a Muslim council was established and my brother was its president. This was a circle of intellectuals who prepared a series of documents --

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I'm going to add my voice to that of Mr. Karnavas. The witness is being non-responsive to the question and clearly is taking advantage of each question to say exactly what he wishes, and he'll have the opportunity to do so, but it's important that it should be done one step at a time, and I ask that Mr. Scott please proceed by way of question and answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Scott, if you're asking questions, it's for us to get to the documents. So the witness must answer in such a way that we know whether the documents are linked to him, either by way of his being the author or because of the contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if you will put exhibit -- I guess what -- we can do it differently. If you will put Exhibit 1376 aside for the time being, or mechanically, technologically, put it aside, and we'll do this a different way. When you were activated by -- as a member of the military police, how long did you continue to act in that position?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: Well, officially I did not hold that position for a long time because it was not possible. And in order to avoid any conflicts, we did not activate the military police. And the way I worked was to send the records to the Ministry of the Interior and to the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina from the field so as to keep Sarajevo informed. Maybe from the 16th of June or, rather --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The gentleman does not wish to answer questions. I understand he's a politician, and I'm trying to be fair. God knows I want to be fair to the gentleman, but he has to answer questions. Now, Mr. Scott is struggling here. I'd like to help him out: Who, what, where, why, how?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm not struggling, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, it seems to be struggling. He can ask chronologically, and maybe we can make it easier for the gentleman. We don't need to hear all this other stuff, but he can go step-by-step. The question was: How long? Now, he can tell us, and then the next question is: How were you able to carry out your function? And then he can go into a long narration. And then what did you do? And then what happened next? That's how direct examination's done. It's simple, it's by the book: Who, what, where, why, how? Describe and explain. That's it. Nothing complicated about this. But the gentleman must answer the questions. We're going to hit -- you're going to have an opportunity to tell his entire story, but it has to be fair to us as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Scott, try to put questions to the witness so that he can tell us exactly when he was the commander of the military police. First, it would be interesting to know who appointed him to that position. We'd like to know which period was concerned, why he didn't exercise his duties, et cetera, et cetera. So try to go in chronological order, if possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And if the witness doesn't provide you with a clear answer to your question, put the question to him again. Try to make sure that the witness doesn't go off on a tangent.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I appreciate all this assistance -- all the assistance I'm getting in the courtroom, Your Honour, having done this for some many, many years, 27 years, but I'll try to do better, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, we'll go back. We'll go back to the very beginning and we will take it one step and one day at a time if we have to. You said that at some time during -- and it's left the page now. If you can please look at the -- I was going to say the page but you don't have that page any more. When were you first activated as a member of the police?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: On the 12th June, 1992. Appointed to that position by Commander Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And how long did you continue in that position, sir? [B/C/S on English channel].

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: Officially, I was never relieved of that office but I reported. I sent regular reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what was your actual position at that time? You said you were first activated as a member of the police. Were you a -- what we might all a line -- a line police officer or what position did you hold as of the 12th of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: Apart from that, I maintained a direct line with the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia -- of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I sent regular reports to the minister, who at that time was Jusuf Pusina, the minister of the interior, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: As guided by the president, please listen and answer specifically my question. My question to you: What was your position as of the 12th of June, 1992? Did you have a rank; were you a commander, were you a captain? That's the only question I'm asking you at this moment.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: At that time, I was just an ordinary operative worker who sent regular reports to the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I was promoted to the rank of officer, I believe, in 1996 only.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What was the nature of these reports that you've told us you were sending to the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and whose direction or to who were you sending those reports?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: I sent these reports to the Ministry of the Interior, to General Sefer Halilovic, meaning also the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and to political leadership of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier -- and I just use this simply as a benchmark and then we can go forward or backwards depending on your answer. You mentioned some pages ago in the transcript that at one point you approached Mate Boban about forming a joint HVO-Muslim police force. Do you recall that? My first question is: Do you recall when you said that earlier?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And approximately when did you have this conversation or meeting with Mr. Boban?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: When I received the order that I would be made commander on the 20th of June, 1992. I went for talks to Grude where Mate Boban was, and Mr. Maric as his secretary. This took place in a hotel, and I believe it is down there by or in the bowling alley. Apart from them, Senad Saja was with me where we talked about the resubordination of the military police of the HVO to the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina to legal organs, and Mate Boban refused that, and he --

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the question was, "Approximately when did you have this conversation with Mr. Boban?" May we please have the next question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said on the 20th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You can --

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: At the hotel in Grude.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I will ask the next question. You had this meeting with Mr. Boban and you've already described it to us now, at least in part, twice. I won't ask you to repeat it again except to tell us -- tell us what Mr. Boban's response was to your proposition that the HVO police should be subordinate to the police of Bosnia and Herzegovina. What was his response to that?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: Mr. Boban's response was that he did not recognise the leadership in Sarajevo, that he did not recognise the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that this would be the state of the Croats, the so-called HZ HB, that he would not recognise anything coming from Sarajevo, and he offered to me what I just said a while ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What did he offer to you, because I'm not sure if we got that or not. What did he offer to you?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: Mr. Boban offered me to choose any position within the HZ HB, to choose a flat in Croatia because I have two children, and as he knew that I was a karate sportist and so were his nephews, he said that he would provide for me. And I said, no, never. I said, however, that it would be good to have a joint police between the Croatian and the Muslim police, and I also said that it was good because Coric Valentin was my pupil, was on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we may have a point of clarification, Your Honour, just for the record, and I'm sure that Your Honours are probably interested. He indicated that he was an operative worker. That's what he was back on 12 June, 1992. Appointed, I assume, by Halilovic and not until 1996 when he got the rank of officer. Then he went on to say that he would be made a commander and that's why he went to see Mate Boban on 20th of June in 1992. I guess the question is what rank is he at that point in time? Is he still an operative worker? Who sent him there? On what basis is he there? I think these are very critical, because obviously we want to check all of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I've noticed that he was rapidly promoted, but in 1996, given that initially he was an operative worker -- well, it was in 1996 that he became an officer. So perhaps there is something that ought to be clarified here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Cupina, I don't know if it's partly -- if there are some problems with translation going on or you and I are just having a problem communicating. If it's my fault, I apologise for that. You said a moment ago when you were appointed as a police officer, activated as police officer in June of 1992, or when you were first -- excuse me, when you were first activated, you held the rank of, if I can use the term, a line police officer. You were a police officer without any particular higher rank, not captain, not anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Excuse me. First of all, this is leading, and secondly he said he was an operative worker. I mean, there's a difference. I don't know what an operative worker is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, maybe if Mr. Karnavas would let me ask a couple of questions, I can get there, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He can ask an open-ended question. He's telling him now, "You were a line police officer."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's what he told us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cupina, you said that you were an operative worker. What does that mean exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I try to explain this very slowly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the war police station which was called Carina and which encompassed almost half of the city, I was one of the leaders, meaning that in this station I had a position of leadership. After that, as I was now ranking and as we were, as members of the Patriotic League, associated with the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and sought to bring Bosnia-Herzegovina to recognition by the United Nations, we didn't have any ranking. Ranking was introduced only later, and I believe that I was conferred a rank by the -- by a decision of the Presidency. What counted for me was to do my patriotic duty for Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you -- when you were the chief of the military police station, did you have a rank or were you just acting as chief there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was just performing a function, an office, because at that time, as far as I know, there were no ranks, there was no ranking. We were just issued orders to perform such-and-such duty without being conferred any rank. That was the situation in Sarajevo. Apart from the order, I didn't get any rank.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you were acting as chief. Did you have a military uniform or civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wore a military uniform at the time, which I changed depending on the need.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But when one is a member of the army, one has a rank. One is a general, an ordinary soldier, a private, an officer, a non-commissioned officer. You had no rank of any kind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I had no rank. I was a commander of the Patriotic League of the city of Mostar, inter alia, but there were no ranks at the time. I was only given to understand that I was the commander of the police region of Mostar, encompassing the whole region of Herzegovina. This was the police organisation at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How many members of the military police did you have beneath you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not have any military police. Because of the impossibility to cooperate with the HVO, the government in Sarajevo would not allow the operative side, the so-called HZ HB, to capitalise on that situation for conflicts. So I did my work there as best as I could, which is to say sent written reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we have understood this correctly, you are responsible for the Patriotic League. You were appointed as chief of the military police, but you say that you didn't have any policemen under you. And then you went to see Mr. Boban, and you told him that you were the chief of the military police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I received -- when we received this order, we were supposed to agree with the HVO about the establishment of the military police, but the HVO did not accept that. And then I informed the government in Sarajevo, and I made a staffing schedule which I sent via Mr. Spago from Konjic, but we never got a concrete answer. Only we were told that this would be done when times were better, but that we were to do everything to prevent the situation from escalating into a conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you received an order from Mr. Halilovic and he appointed you as chief of the military police in the Mostar area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Scott, please proceed and let's try to see things clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, confirm for us, when did you receive the appointment from Mr. Halilovic as chief of the military police, the question that the president just put to you. Approximately when was that?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: 12th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, were you -- is that the position that you held as of January and February, 1993? If not, then I'll ask you to explain to us any different -- what had happened and what different position you held.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: Until the end of the war, I was never relieved of this office in written form, but I always maintained contacts with the political, legislative, executive, and judicial authorities in Sarajevo, and I collected documents and reported on all developments in Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But in order to carry out your duties, were you alone or were you assisted by anyone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I was discharging that duty, we had our people in the Muslim council of Herzegovina who were intellectuals, and they set up expert teams which compiled -- compiled reports on developments in HZ HB, which was -- and then the members in the Patriotic League were always the -- under pressure from the HZ HB, gave us reports to refer them on to Sarajevo, both from the Ministry of the Interior and from the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, you mentioned breaking at 20 to 4.00. If you'd like to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just for the record, that's a non-response response. It's not responding to the question. I mean, what was he doing? I guess, Mr. President, your question was very specific. I mean, it seems to me it's a one-man military police for the entire Herzegovina region, and he's not being concrete, and perhaps because there maybe some confabulation, I dare say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you have studied, you're a deputy right now, so you understand the question. You say that you were the chief of the military police. If that's the case, then one has to carry out investigations. One has to forward these investigations to the military prosecutor if there is a military prosecutor. One has to compile reports and forward them to the Ministry of Defence or to the Ministry of the Interior. And similarly one has to work within a certain frame work, within an certain established structure, and now you're telling us that you had certain intellectuals who provided you with assistance. I must say that I have absolutely no idea as to what sort of tasks you carried out in your capacity as chief of the military police. Is there anything you could tell us to clarify what the exact nature of your position was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The military -- it was impossible to form the military police in order to avoid a conflict. This position of mine remained. It was a vacancy but it was never filled, if you understand me. After that, I regularly went to Sarajevo and I saw people from the legislative and executive branches of authority and I sent reports about the situation in Herzegovina. Practically, in practice, the military police could not be set up without a conflict erupting, which is what the HZ HB wanted. They threatened that if we were to set up the military police, that they would create conflicts. So that is why we did not establish one. I sent reports as operative reports, as I've said, to Sarajevo via satellite telephone or via courier about all developments in Herzegovina, and I even went to Sarajevo myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And did you have an office of your own, a telephone, an address?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not have an office. I did not have an address. We kept changing places because of the repression by the HVO because they persecuted everyone who was working for Bosnia and Herzegovina, and in particular people who were working to set up districts because it was an obligation to set up a district of Mostar according to the regulations, the republican regulations of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So we did not have military police in the sense of having prisons, nor did we want any prisons, but the HVO did set up such prisons, which was contrary to regulations in Bosnia-Herzegovina. We did not want to have that kind of a structure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You name yourself commander and a commander is someone who commands and there must be something to command. In fact you seem not to have been anything like a commander. Were you not rather something under the title, perhaps, of commander, like a secret agent, a kind of a spy, and maybe a shadow, potential commander? Was that your position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My position was exactly like this: I was to analyse the entire situation in the territory of Herzegovina and Mostar and to inform people, because they wouldn't let us set up a military police. The HVO wouldn't let us, and the HZ HB wouldn't let us. They threatened us with death, with repercussions and reprisals, and so on and so forth, because they themselves had formed all these structures already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is another question that one of the Judges would like to put to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I would just like to try and understand the situation you were in at the time. There was a government that had been established in Sarajevo, and the government gave you the task of establishing the military police, and you had the position of commander, but this was never an effective position. You never had any policemen or soldiers who were under you because the HVO had its own forces present in the area. Is that in fact your explanation? You were, in a certain sense, a member of the resistance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exactly. The HVO wouldn't allow the forming of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It wouldn't allow the forming of the military police of Bosnia and Herzegovina, especially not for the region of Mostar. The region of Mostar did not exist in their book. It was the so-called HZ HB. It was not Herzegovina. But that was in keeping with their regulations of the creation of their HZ HB state. And I was one of the greatest enemies, if such a state was structured and organised, that is. Our people thought that we should not escalate the conflict by seeking the formation of these structures so that we would desist from that idea. You can see in the video footage that I was with all the officials during the war period in the area of Herzegovina, starting with President Izetbegovic and then with Zlatko Lagumdzija, with all people who were trying to help Bosnia-Herzegovina remain a state in every possible positive way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll have the break now and we will resume at 4.10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, with the background of the last half hour, let me go back to specifically the time period January and February of 1993. Do you understand the time period that I'm focusing on, January, February, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, can you tell the Judges very concisely, in a short and direct answer, what were you doing in Mostar? What were your responsibilities, if any, if you held any official post? What were your responsibilities in and around Mostar as of that specific time period, January, February, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: In January and February, 1993, I gathered information on the events, on the negative acts of the so-called HZ HB in the territory of Herzegovina, and I carried out these duties, as I have already said, as a policeman and member of the army. In September, 1992, I handed over some material to the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was in Zagreb. I continued to gather material so as to inform about the overall situation in Mostar, about the political, legislative, and judicial situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, in --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: If I may, just for the record. There is nothing in the statement of the witness -- 20 January statement, nothing about January and February, 1993. So it's an entirely new subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, we had this discussion earlier today. I don't know if we have to have the same discussion again. The statements were disclosed, the documents were disclosed, and the documents are, which they've all had for months, were included in what's been disclosed and what's in the Prosecution exhibit list. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, in this particular capacity, did you provide any information, documentation to either Mr. Campara, Mr. Hamdija Jahic, or to Mr. Sead Maslo during that time period?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Let me ask the witness to wait for a moment. I would only like to clarify one issue there in -- in actually in lines - let me see - 13 and 14 -- 12, 14. It was written and also I heard in the translation that, "In September, 1992, I handed over some material to the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was in Zagreb." I believe that the witness was probably had in mind not Zagreb but Sarajevo. I don't know if it is the case, so probably the transcript could be clarified and -- and corrected in this respect. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I? I did hand it over to Zagreb because Mr. Alija Izetbegovic was in Zagreb as well as the Vice Prime Minister, Zlatko Lagumdzija. There was Alija Spahic, Jusuf Pusina, and the Minister of Development Dizdarevic, and that was the first time that I provided all documents on what was being done by the HZ HB in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina to the official government of Bosnia and Herzegovina. After that, I went on a trip in the free territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina with Mr. Zlatko Lagumdzija.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, going back to my question then, during this time period January, February of 1993, were you providing -- talk about gathering information and providing reports? Did you provide information, documentation to either Mr. Campara, Mr. Jahic, or Mr. Maslo?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: As for Mr. Campara, Mr. Jahic, and Mr. Maslo, well, we are friends and we would exchange information on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... my question was did you provide them with any information? And you either did or you didn't.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what -- now, will you tell us about your relationship with these -- one or more of these gentlemen, whichever ones you were associated with at that time.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: We were friends and all three of them worked on the protection of the AVNOJ border in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, can I ask the registrar to please display to you again Exhibit P 01376.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And while that is being done, Your Honour, just for the record again, in the gentleman's statement there is a gap between April, 1992, in paragraph 8.
