In paragraph 9 it then begins with 9 May -- May 9 and May 28, 1993. There is a complete gap for that period. And so to point -- as Mr. Kovacic has indicated, this is on new material. Any documentation regarding -- that was -- that is between that period we would object to being introduced because we have actually no reason to believe that this gentleman was associated with anything with respect to any papers during that period of time, during the gap period. There is absolutely nothing to describe what the gentleman was doing. This is all brand new.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, again, apparently counsel, when they read the witness statement --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Just a minute. Could we first establish whether this is a document? Then we can decide whether we should linger on this document and whether we should use it with this witness. The witness said that all the signatories were still alive, but this document hasn't been signed. I would like to draw your attention to that fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Scott. You were going to ask the witness a question about a document that --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm sure that all the counsel on the other side have wonderful ideas on how I should conduct cross-examination [sic], but one has one idea, another has another idea. I have to ask a series of questions. One question probably won't ask all the questions, but if we can proceed -- if I can be allowed to proceed as best I can, as poorly as that might be, I would appreciate being able to move forward on that. In response to the questions, however, Your Honour, that's been raised by Mr. Karnavas -- the issue raised by Mr. Karnavas, again, Your Honour, I don't know. I don't know what the problem is. Mr. Kovacic has said, yes, in fact we've had this statement for a long time. No problem with that. No problems at all. Now, perhaps they didn't read the last page of the statement, page 8, which specifically lists these documents. Annex I, dated February, 1993, Analysis of the State Administration, et cetera, et cetera. Annex J, February, 1993, Proposal to the Commission Within the Board for State Government Administration. Now, that's in his statement. I don't know what the problems are when they say this is not in the statement. There it is, and the documents were provided and the Defence have had those documents for a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting that we did not -- that the statement does not reflect that documents were attached or presented by this gentleman to the OTP. What I'm saying is in the narrative, in the witness's statement there is a jump between April, 1992, and 9 May, 1993. There is nothing there for that period. The rest -- and this is on page 2. The rest -- which is where the statement begins. For the rest of the statement, it covers the period post-May, 1993. Now we're being referenced to a document that is of February, 1993. There is absolutely nothing in his testimony as to what he was doing, nothing that would link the gentleman during that period of time. That's what we're pointing out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, ask the witness what he was doing between April and May, but I do believe that he has already answered that question, but ask him to repeat his answer to tell us what he was doing in April and May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Witness, you've heard the question. Mr. Cupina, can you tell the Judges, please, and again please answer specifically the question, please be concise and direct. What were your activities in April and May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: April, 1992, to May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm reading from the transcript, and that's what Judge Antonetti asked for. Perhaps you would like to correct Judge Antonetti. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, you are well aware that in the statement between paragraphs 8 and 9 there is a gap. That's the gap that I'm referring to. There was no testimony, nothing was given by this witness to the investigator. Documents were presented. I have no objections to the documents being going through, but I think we need to know what the gentleman was doing during this period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, it's very simple: Between April, 1992, until May, 1993, as far as you can remember, are you able to tell us what position you held and what duties you carried out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Between April, 1992, I was the president for the commission -- from May, 1993, I was the president for the exchange of prisoners. In April, I was a soldier, like everyone else, and I was involved in the defence of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I was on the left bank, and we did everything that was necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your permission, let's start with April, 1992. In April, 1992, what were you doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'll be very brief. From April, 1992, onwards, I was first the commander of the Independent Battalion for the defence of Mostar. That was in April, 1992. On the 12th of June, 1992, I was the commander of the military police in the Mostar region. As of that date, until when I was appointed as the president of the commission, I held that position. I didn't lose that position. I wasn't dismissed from that position. After having held that position, I was a commissioner for Mostar, a commissioner for Energopetrol. That was in July, 1993, I think.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The witness mentioned the date the 12th of the 16th, 1992. He probably meant the 12th of the 6th, or the 12th of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, again, we've lost the transcript on the page, but were you providing -- did you provide information around this time to Mr. -- Either Mr. Campara, Mr. Jahic, or Mr. Maslo?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what was your relationship or -- at that time with these three individuals? I mean from a professional perspective. You told us you were collecting information. From the activities that you were engaged in at that time, what was your relationship with these three individuals?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: An exceptional relationship, because before the war Maslo was the republican inspector for administrative and legal affairs, and Mr. Jahic was in the Executive Board of the Municipal Assembly of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: How about Mr. Campara --

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: Similarly, Mr. Campara was also in that situation. We had known each other for a long time, we were all in Mostar, and we found ourselves in a similar position for the defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, if you can look at Exhibit P 01376. If you still have that in front of you or not. Do you recognise that document, sir?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell us very briefly, what is that document as you know it?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: Well, it's an analysis of the situation, administrative situation of the state and the territory of Herzegovina and how to establish the legal authorities. There was an analysis of the administrative structure before the war and of what happened when the HZ HB was established. We know who was the president of the Assembly, who the vice-president of the Assembly was at the time: Milivoj Gagro was the president of the Assembly, the President of the Executive Board was Bajric, then Mumin Isic was the secretary.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you there, sir. You've answered my question. Did you provide information and documentation to the three gentlemen named previously for the purposes of them preparing this report?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you participate, sir, in the preparation of this report, then?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: Well, in an indirect way, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in what indirect way?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: In a direct way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maslo and Jahic would often come to see me in my flat and we'd try to agree on how to draft this and how to draft this in accordance with a legal document. It's because I was an economist.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Your Honour, just for clarification's sake, one the reasons I asked the follow-up question was what was indicated as the answer but has been corrected. The witness said he was involved in the preparation of the report in a direct way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, what did you understand the purpose of this report was and -- well, let's take it that first. What did you understand the purpose of the preparation of this report was?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: The purpose was to analyse the entire situation before the war, in the course of the war, and when the HZ HB was established in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, or, rather, when this entity, the HZ HB and the HVO were established.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell us, sir, was this report then transmitted to someone or something?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: Well, as I've already said, it was translated to Sarajevo, to the Ministry of the Interior, or, rather, to the government. They had all those reports. We sent reports to the government and also to Jusuf Halilovic, who was in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you recall who in the government in -- in the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Sarajevo? Do you have any recollection of the particular individual or individuals who received this report when it was transmitted?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: It was sent to the Ministry of the Interior. It was sent directly there, and I told Mr. Jusuf Halilagic about it. He was a republican inspector for administrative and legal affairs. Before the war he was based in Zenica, and I asked him to forward it to the government once he had received it. So it went through two channels.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I next ask the ushers to show you -- the usher to show you, please, Exhibit P 01619. Sir, can you tell us if you recognise that document; and if the answer is yes, can you tell the Judges what the document is.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: Yes. It's an analysis of the current authority in Mostar municipality. On the 9th of April, the municipality of Mostar had already been occupied by the so-called JNA, and naturally by other formations, the SDS, and formations from Serbia and Montenegro. They appealed to the decision on withdrawing the JNA units from the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and this was a decision adopted on the 27th of April, 1992, by the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and having appealed to this decision, the Crisis Staff of Mostar, which was to all intents and purposes the Executive Board of the municipality of Mostar, on the 29th of April they adopted a decision according to which government authority should be handed over to the HVO. However, it's quite clear that not all powers handed over. Later on, a commission for special purposes was formed and then they made -- then they set up a putsch in the HZ HB.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Would you look, please, at the last page of the document P 01619, and tell us who prepared the report and if that's one of the same individuals listed on the previous report.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: Yes. This document was compiled by Sead Maslo. The document refers to the events that transpired during that period of time. Unfortunately, a military putsch was carried out and the HVO of the HZ HB took over and the legal authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina no longer functioned, in fact, from the 15th of May, 1992, onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In -- you're saying in Mostar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: Yes, yes, in Mostar. I'm talking about Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, on this report did you have anything to do with the preparation of this report? Did you provide information to Mr. Maslo? Did you provide documentation to him?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: Mr. Maslo cooperated with me on a daily basis. We provided each other with reports, and we cooperated with each other and we forwarded them, naturally, to institutions that were responsible for such matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court, who was this report transmitted to?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: The report was forwarded to the government again, and it was sent to Jusuf Halilagic. All the reports were forwarded to Jusuf Halilagic in the republic, the inspector for legal affairs. And if we couldn't provide the reports, it was his responsibilities to provide the reports to the legal organs of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just so the record is clear, when you say this man was the -- an inspector for republican and legal affairs - I'm just looking at the transcript - which particular ministry or agency or authority was he part of?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: Before the war he worked in the Ministry of Justice and now he's the secretary of the Ministry of Justice of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You mean at the present time?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: Now he is the secretary, and before the war he was the republican inspector for administrative and legal affairs. I think that was the name of that department.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So this was in the Ministry of Justice at the time these reports were being communicated to him; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's leading, and that's not what the gentleman answered. He was asked twice. So the question is what is he doing during the war, not before and after.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That was my question back to you, sir. When you said you were transmitting this report to this gentleman on line -- page 55, line 6, you referred to him as the inspector. For which ministry was he working at that point in time --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, it assumes -- again it assumes that he's working for a particular ministry. He can just ask the question: Who is he working for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Yes. For the Ministry of Administrative and Legal Affairs, as far as I know. And all these documents were the Constitutional Court in September, 1992, as evidence in order to annul the decisions of the so-called HZ HB, because these were crucial documents with regard to what took place in Mostar and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you to please to be -- let me ask you to please be shown Exhibit P 00219. Sir, can you tell the Judges whether this was one of the documents that you gathered and collected and passed on to these other gentleman writing these reports at that time?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: Yes. For a certain period of time these people were in the Municipal Council in July: Hamdija Jahic, Senad Kazazic, Sead Maslo. This was the proposal of the SDA. And when they saw that these documents didn't have to do with the -- well, they -- they resigned on the 3rd of August, 1992, when they saw what these documents were about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you'll stop there for a moment, please. Who resigned?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: Senad Kazazic. I think that he was responsible for reconstruction, development. Then Sead Maslo, then Hamdija Jahic. These were the individuals who resigned. There was Mumin Isic as well. The 3rd of August they resigned from the SDA and the letters I transmitted to the government that was in Zagreb at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may interrupt for a second. The gentleman is being shown P 0219. What I seem to have is somewhat different. It doesn't have any of these names. Perhaps I'm mistaken, but my colleague and I are -- are a little perplexed. What is exactly the gentleman referring to, and what document?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: He wasn't referring to that -- Your Honour, my understanding of his testimony - I'm sure I'll be corrected - is that he recognised the document, and he mentioned that as/when this document became known to a number of people over the next period of time until August of 1992, these people then resigned their positions on the basis of becoming aware of these developments. That's what I understood his testimony to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could you look -- could I please ask the witness to be shown Exhibit P 00485.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. Is the witness identifying the last exhibit, number 219? I'm not sure whether he authenticated or identified it or not at this point, so perhaps that could be clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I believe he testified, Your Honour, this is one of the documents that he had collected and provided to the people preparing the report. I believe that's what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, perhaps you should ask him whether the document P 219 is one he was aware of or whether the persons under Article I were relieved of duty before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. Give me a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, rather to take the time, sir, to find it -- try to find it in the record, let me ask you: Is Exhibit P 00219, is that a document that you had collected around this time and provided to Mr. Maslo and others at the time that they were preparing their report?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour, but I have to acknowledge that I have a great deal of problems in following all this. The witness should remember that he is under oath, under the solemn declaration. He said he sent these documents to the official authorities who discussed them when the decisions of the Constitutional Court were taken in 1992. From the reports, we can see that they were sent in in February, 1993. The witness is now showing us another document in which Mr. Maslo and Jahic, he says, took part in the body that he's talking about now. Now, I really don't know whether the witness has mixed everything up, which is quite probable, or is he not telling the truth to this Court? I can't follow his testimony at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, again I think that's an overstatement. I agree it perhaps isn't the clearest testimony that one could wish for, but I believe that what was said was he collected a number of documents, he's confirmed the documents as they've been shown to him, and then he has gone on -- then he has gone on to add a number of other pieces of information about that. As I understood what he said about the document in the Constitutional Court, he said these were very important documents that I gathered they were later transmitted to the government and were in relation to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Document P 219, the one we have on our screens, sir, take a look at that. You have it on the screen. It is the document. It is a decision signed by Mr. Topic on the 21st of May, 1992. Now, this particular document, who did you hand it over to, send it to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I've already said that all the documents that I gathered I sent to the government -- handed over to the government in Zagreb. And I also said that the people who at the time were appointed by the SDA gave statements that they no longer wished to be in the government, because the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was being overthrown, and I handed that over. And then I said that they were documents which later on the Constitutional Court would take as valid and would challenge all the HZ HB decisions working on the territory of Herzegovina and Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. We're at zero again. You say that you handed over this document to Sarajevo and that you also transmitted it to the persons whose names were mentioned a moment ago, and then you added that these documents allowed the -- the contents of them allowed the Constitutional Court to make its ruling, to render its decision.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is one of the documents that were evidence to prove that Bosnia-Herzegovina was being overthrown. That's just one of the documents to prove that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How do you know about that, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I know that because all this was contrary to the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was common knowledge how the executive powers were established. And there was a putsch by the HZ HB, and these were all illegal decisions of Bosnia-Herzegovina. None of them relied upon the laws and bylaws of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So that is your own interpretation of that, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is the interpretation given by all the legal men, all the lawyers; that all these documents were largely contrary to the laws and legal provisions of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott -- yes, Mr. Ibrisimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. In paragraph 21, the Prosecution says that the Constitutional Court decision was brought in far before the witness having mentioned this document and -- as having been provided to the Constitutional Court. So in fact, the Constitutional Court could not have used this document at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are two decisions of the Constitutional Court, the first one declaring illegal and unconstitutional the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and the second decision declaring illegal and unconstitutional the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. Both of those decisions are in evidence already. They've been admitted. I don't know off the top of my head the exhibits numbers. I'm sure if I have a moment I can look them up, if necessary. And the timing of those will be apparent on their face; one was earlier, the second one was later.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but Mr. Scott is now testifying instead of the witness. The witness said that the decision was taken in 1992, and we know that for sure, that this decision does not relate to the Republic of Herceg-Bosna. So the witness said, I sent off the material which helped the Constitutional Court to make its decision in 1992. And the material is dated -- the documents are dated 1993. And I am telling you what the record reflects and what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, the Constitutional Court made two decisions. To the best of your recollection, the documents that you sent to -- or took to Sarajevo, were they before the two decisions taken by the Constitutional Court? Was that before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, what you've just said here, that dates to the 21st of May, 1992, this particular document. And as far as I can see on the screen, that is the date, the 21st of May, 1992. I see no other document in front of me here. That's the only document that I can see on my screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And to the best of your recollections, the Constitutional Court decisions were made at what date, on what date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 19th of September, 1992. That was the first decision. And the second decision I can't remember exactly what date that was. I think it was the 19th of September, 1992. That one I remember. I think that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour, but I don't want it to appear that I am intentionally causing a misunderstanding. The witness has spoken about the second document now, but he also said that he sent document 01376, which is an analysis of the state -- state administration in Herzegovina, how to establish a legal authority in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and he said that he sent that to the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Zagreb, that he handed it over. And I'm saying that that document is February, 1993, that that's the date of it. He said documents in the plural and did not refer to a document in the singular.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be allowed to explain?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You want to say that the Constitutional Court took its decision in September, 1992. It would appear that document -- your brother-in-law's document was drafted in February, 1993. Therefore, that is posterior to the decision of September, after the September decision.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me tell you, I'm talking about the first decision made by the Constitutional Court. To avoid any misunderstanding, that is these documents that I took to Zagreb. Now, as far as the other decisions are concerned, I took them to Sarajevo. Because there was a meeting of the government in the Palace Hotel, and I was there. So that was for the first decision. As for the other decisions, they were taken to Sarajevo or Zenica. I don't want to lead to any misunderstandings here. I'm not very well-versed in matters -- or don't have the habit of testifying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just for the record, Your Honour, in terms of the comment that I was testifying, I was responding specifically to the question raised by Mr. Ibrisimovic, and I take it Mr. Ibrisimovic was not testifying either, but I was responding to the objection that he raised, and that's the reason for my statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, can I ask you to be shown, please, Exhibit P 00485. Do you have that in front of you, sir? Can you look at that just enough to recognise what it is, and if you do recognise it, can you tell the Judges what it is.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: This document I do recognise, yes. It is the decision to delete the words "Territorial Defence" in all the documents of the Croatian Defence Council because they considered that to be linked to Serbia and Montenegro, and they didn't even give -- allow us to form the Territorial Defence, which was a department in the Kamena building in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell the Judges, is this a document that you gathered and provided in reports, either directly or indirectly, to the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to move your attention forward, please, to approximately May of 1993. Can you tell the Judges, please, around that time, did you become a member of a certain commission? And if your answer is yes, I will ask at the end that you describe what the commission was.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What commission were you appointed to at that time?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: The president for the Commission of the Exchange of Soldiers and Civilians of the 4th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And who placed you in that position?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: Officially, I never saw that document, but I received information according to which President Izetbegovic had established a commission which was outside the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and a commission in Mostar as well. So they informed me about that. Commander Pasalic said that he and I would take part as president of the Commission for the Exchange of Soldiers and Civilians of the 4th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Would you briefly tell the Judges what kind of activities this commission then became involved in in approximately May of 1993.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: The commission was involved in gathering all individuals together, all those arrested by the HVO on the territory of Mostar and further afield in the region because the HVO, on the 9th of May, attacked, and we had no information about the elderly, women, and children. And we tried to ask the parents of children to give us the names and surnames of their children, which concentration camps their nearest and dearest were to be found.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Witness, you have just used the word, the term "concentration camp." Was that the normal terminology at the time you were acting as the president of that commission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let me tell you. As far as we were concerned, it was a concentration camp, because to take someone from their own home, to abuse them, rape them, beat them, and subject them to various torture, take them to the Heliodrom, which already in June, 1992, was prepared to take in and abuse people like that kind, kill them, rape them and so on, keep them without food, everything that was contrary to civilisational trends.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ibrisimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, perhaps there's an error in the transcript, but it remains unclear who was the president of the commission; Mr. Pasalic or the witness or both of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Answer that, please, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let me tell you. You saw in the text that it was first signed by Pasalic, and underneath his signature there is my signature. But as he had combat assignments and assignments elsewhere, he asked me to act as president, although in the document it says that he was the president of the commission. And on the other side, you have the other names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the commission, did it have any offices, premises, headquarters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the commission did have an office in the main street, and it was Marsal Tito Street, opposite the social accounting service building. It had an office there and there it had a number of staff, about seven employees, two women among them. I think there was Mr. Pitic and Mr. Zulovic, then there was Jakirovic, and Pijavica [phoen], Saric, and so on. I don't want to name all the names now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the people who were employed, who were they paid by?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it was like this: We had no water, no electricity, the BH dinar was prohibited. We had nothing. We had no humanitarian aid. We were just captured there in that enclave, under siege from all sides, and we did our best to survive. So nobody thought about salaries or I don't know what money could have been used to pay us in any way. No, we received no salaries. We weren't paid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If the registry can please show you Exhibit P 02344. Can you tell, sir, what this document is and, if so, how it relates to your work on this commission.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: As far as I can see from this on the screen, it is a document on the basis of which we compiled another document. This is an agreement in Medjugorje between Mr. Sefer Halilovic and Mr. Milivoj Petkovic, and on that basis we received instructions about what we were supposed to do. That's as far as I'm able to see from this. To conduct an exchange, all for all. And we compiled a document like that. Not the one on our screens, but anyway, it followed on from this document, the one that we're looking at now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, that's my question. What did you do, then, to engage, to implement the agreed exchange or exchanges?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: When we were told of the agreement, when the agreement was reached, I think in the building of what was formerly the lottery of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the premises of another centre, regional centre, we met there with HV representatives, with the European Monitors, military and civilian. You have their names and surnames. We compiled a document to conduct an exchange, all for all, and that all people, especially civilians, women and children, should be released from the concentration camps. And as far as I remember, we had nobody who was captured at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What was the name of the commission that you worked on at this time, specifically in May, 1993, if you recall the name of the commission?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: The commission was for the exchange of soldiers and civilians. The 4th Corps Commission for Exchange of Soldiers and Civilians. That's what it was called.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for clarification: Can we take it that the witness is authenticating or identifying this document between General Petkovic and General Halilovic which appears on our screens in English and that he is able to identify and authenticate it? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document, Witness, did you have knowledge of it when you presided with Pasalic over the commission for the exchange of prisoners? Did you know about the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let me tell you. Mr. Sefer Halilovic, I think, came to the left bank on the sixth day and then went to Medjugorje and had a meeting there with Mr. Milivoj Petkovic, and he informed us that this agreement had been reached so that we could go ahead and work on the ground in the territory. I think that he came with him on that occasion, and Bojadzic was there too. He was a brigadier. When we received that information, UNPROFOR arranged a meeting on the territory of the HVO, and they continued work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You say as we were informed. Who informed you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was informed by General Pasalic. General Pasalic informed me. He had direct links.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Pasalic had met General Petkovic and General Halilovic, had he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whether they met or not I don't know. It was my job to accept it and start implementing it. That is to say UNPROFOR was the mediator. We never had any direct links. It was the international community who acted as the go-between.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Could you answer the president's question as to this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may intervene.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Did you ever see this? May I ask this question?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: There is a problem with the translation of what's on the screen, Your Honour, so the witness may not be seeing the correct document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That's another matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I've been informed, please, that there may be a translation or loading error in e-court and what the document has on the screen -- what the witness has on the screen may not be the appropriate document or the translation, which may indeed account for some of the confusion in the last few minutes. Could -- I am told that at the end of the document 00481493 is the B/C/S version of this document. Page 4 of the document, the B/C/S document starts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The record should reflect that the gentleman was answering questions from Mr. Scott based on what was on his screen. What was on his screen was English. So either he was making it up or either there's -- I don't know what to make of it, but obviously -- does the gentleman read English? He was shown an English document from which he was testifying. So if he doesn't read English, how can he possibly validate a document and testify from it? I mean, it just defies logic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Wait a minute. Wait a minute. Mr. Karnavas always jumps to the worst possible interpretation of an event. Always.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: His task.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I assume -- we can ask the witness if we need to. My goodness. The witness can probably read the names Petkovic and Halilovic. He can probably read the date. In the context of the questions being put to him he probably figured out what the document was. Now, until just a few minutes ago, since it wasn't on my screen and I wasn't alerted to the fact that the right document wasn't on the screen, so can we have a little bit of reasonable flexibility in terms of courtroom procedure. The witness was shown the document. Now apparently it's on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps he understands English. Do you understand English, sir? Do you know English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Enough for me to be able to understand many things that are said, but no, I don't speak English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So a document in English, you could at least get the gist of what it says, could you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in some parts, yes, but not -- I don't speak fluent English and I can't actually say that I understand it all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think that's a fair explanation, Your Honour. He could read enough to know what the document appeared to be to him. That's what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry if I insist. Can the witness now be shown the B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sure, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: -- document and then tell us if he has seen it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Of course. We're there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now that we have the correct document, I hope, sir, on the screen. Well, the one I have -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: No, it's still in English. Now it's good, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be allowed to answer? On the basis of this document we compiled a document the HVO and the BH army. We weren't able to rely on some other document in the presence of European Monitors, military and civilian. So I couldn't have used another document. There was just one document, this one here. I think that's quite understandable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And you did actually see it? You are familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell the Judges, in your involvement with this commission --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honours, but it took me a little time to check it out. We are aware of the document, we've seen it before, but that document was not on the list, on the two lists provided to us by the Prosecution in advance having to do with this witness and his testimony. The Prosecution was very kind as to give us a separate review and to tie up all the documents envisaged for this witness, but it did not include that particular document. We were not told that we were being -- we would be dealing with that document, and this raises a problem for our defence and the preparation of the Defence case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, we will have to check the records. I do not have all these things committed to memory. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Maybe -- [Interpretation] Not to create a misunderstanding, I'm talking about the proofing chart. I'm referring to the proofing chart, and I'm talking about this document here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's not on the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not on either of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... because I've been objecting quite a bit this afternoon, but it's not on there. But if he can establish a foundation, I personally have no objection to the gentleman testifying, but it's not on the list and I think Mr. Kovacic does make a valid point, and I'm sure it might be an oversight on the part of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic has just told us, Mr. Scott, that document P 2344 was not on the proofing chart.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I -- I'll have to -- sorry. I will have to do some additional checking, Your Honour. I'm looking at a document which says "Exhibits for Prosecution witness Suad Cupina," and on that document it is listed on the second page. It is the one, two, three, four, five, sixth item listed on that page. Now, if some page was left out or dropped, or the wrong page was inserted, I can't tell you, Your Honour, without making further inquiries, but I'm looking at a document which specifically lists 2344. I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's not, but it doesn't matter. As I said, if they can lay a foundation, I have no objections to the gentleman testifying about a particular document, as long as they lay a foundation, though we -- we're pretty organised here, as everyone else is, and we just don't have it, but again we're not saying that there's any foul play here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please continue, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, when you were involved in this commission, can you tell us about -- did you meet with counterparts on the other side, that is the HVO, for the purposes of arranging exchanges?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell us who, sir, some the people on the HVO side were that you dealt with during this period?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, Mr. Puljic, I believe, and on our side it was I myself, Mr. Pasalic, and representatives of the international community, but as far as I could see, they only represented numbers there because all the meetings were followed by the Supreme Commanders of the HZ HB HVO from the area of Mostar and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, I don't know what you mean, perhaps others don't either. When you said "they only represented numbers," what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: Well, what I mean, they went out at all times to sort of consult like some sort of office personnel charged with some particular office, clerical duties. People who were not there to say something specifically carried no weight, in other words, and we actually did all the substantive work in all the talks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, may I interrupt you for a moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you. I would only like to ask the witness. He once mentioned that he was the -- if I understood him correctly, that he was at one time, at least, the commander of the Independent Battalion. I would only like to ask you, sir, if you continued to be a commander of the Independent Battalion at that time when this document was signed, that is 12th of May, 1993. Independent Battalion was composed of mainly the Muslim Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness said before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I would like you to clarify if that battalion still existed in 1993. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Independent Battalion was named after an anti-fascist unit celebrated in the Second World War in Mostar. It existed since the beginning of April and on, but at that particular time it did not exist. The 4th Corps and the Mostar Brigade existed on that date, and the 4th Corps, I believe, was formed on the 16th or 17th of November, 1992, and the Mostar Brigade in the beginning of July, 1992, I believe. So that the Independent Battalion actually became part of the Mostar Brigade and the Mostar Brigade, with other units, the 4th Corps. And finally, on the 12th of May, 1993, the 4th Corps and the Mostar Brigade were there with these other formations such as the Independent Battalions, the Pod Velez Battalion, and other units. That's as far as I can recall it now. And the Nevesinje Battalion as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, so far I believe you mentioned, if I heard you correctly, you mentioned dealing with, on the HVO side, Mr. Puljic and Mr. Maric. When you attended these meetings around this time, did anyone else on the HVO side participate in the meetings and conversations about exchanges?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: Well, officially those were the people, but in that room of the H -- everybody who was somebody in the HVO leadership in the Mostar area -- area came in every now and then, into the room, and then they went out. Berto Pusic and all other people who had powers in the connection whatsoever, so that I can't really put my finger on it. I have to say -- I cannot say they were not there. They were there in a way. They, as I said, came in and went out. At a certain point, in fact, Jadran Topic sent everybody out of the meeting room, including international representatives who were signatories of the all-for-all agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Sir, if you'll stop there, please. On the transcript you were going quite quickly. You mentioned the name, at line 24 of page 74, you mentioned the name Pusic. The transcript didn't get the first name. Can you tell us the first name of this individual that you did -- if you do know, and if you did mention it.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: Berto, Berto Pusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you know what his involvement in these matters were at the time?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: I know that he was a member of their National Security Service or what have you, I believe from July, 1992. There were different commissions, three or four commissions there and, inter alia, he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you understand we're talking about May, 1993, not July --

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: Yes, yes. From July he was all of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In May, 1993, what was Mr. Pusic's involvement in these matters?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: He was in constant contact with these two, giving them instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Who's "these two"?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: Maric, Puljic. Should I explain further?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Not yet. Now, you said that they --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'm afraid there is a confusion here. Is the witness referring to one specific event or is he generally describing the situation? I really fail to understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe if we go back into the transcript, we've been talking now about a series of meetings and communications that this witness was involved in during the approximate period May, 1993, and I asked him a number of people -- who he was involved in, and we've come back to it a couple of times and he's mentioned at least three particular individuals now; Mr. Puljic, Mr. Maric, and Mr. Pusic, and he just said that -- he's also mentioned --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Jadran Topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To simplify matters, when you were a member of this commission, did you personally see Mr. Pusic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes. I know -- I know him from the time we were children and young people. I think that Savo Pudar was his friend when they were young.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you knew him. Did you see him at the meeting that concerned prisoner exchange?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On which date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On all those dates when we came for such meetings, he was there throughout that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As of which date was he present at all the meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The report which I made is from May till mid-June. So that should correspond to that period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And when he was there with you and Mr. Pasalic and Mr. Maric, were representatives of the international community also in the hall where meetings were being held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I add? Do you recognise Mr. Pusic in the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, I do. I can. He is over there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know all of them. We all lived in the same city.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd just like to ask another question. How was Mr. Pusic dressed, Mr. Pusic who was in the hall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, he's sitting right by Valentin Coric. I'm still not senile, I hope.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: If the interpreter heard the witness right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He is right there, sitting by that column.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Will you just please say what his first name is. Mr. Pusic's, that is. Just tell us the name of Mr. Pusic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that his name is Berto or Brko Pusic. I know him very well, and I know that this is what they call him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, going back to Judge Mindua's question, I'm afraid he has the same problem as I do. Please listen specifically to the question and answer the question, and I believe Judge Mindua said how was Mr. Pusic dressed, during the time that you were meeting with him, if I understand the question. At the time, how was Mr. Pusic dressed, back in 1993?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: He was wearing an HVO military uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure that was the intent of Judge Mindua's question. I think it was more directed to identification. I don't want to put words into His Honour's mouth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm reading what's in the transcript. Sorry, Your Honour, if I misinterpreted your question. I was reacting to the transcript. In any event, I guess both questions have been answered, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, could I ask you to look at Exhibit P 02512. Do you see that, sir? Do you have that in front of you? Could you tell the Judges what that document is.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: That is the document of the negotiating team to implement a cease-fire agreement in Bosnia-Herzegovina, concluded between General Milivoj Petkovic and General Sefer Halilovic, and here in the preamble we refer to that, and we also indicate the negotiating parties to it. That is a document of the Commission for the Exchange and Liberation of All Civilians in the area of the army of BH; i.e., the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you were asked earlier if you had seen the document, the agreement signed by Mr. Petkovic and Mr. Halilovic. At the top of this document, does this document indicate that it's in -- pursuant to and in reference to that agreement?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: Yes, it does. Yes, and I did see that document, the previous one you referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can the witness please be shown Exhibit P 02882.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But first of all I'd like to go back to document 2512. I'd like to see the last page of this document. Sir, you can see the document before you. How is it that you haven't signed beneath your name?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: Yes, my signature is there under number 2. Yeah, it is there. The commission of the BH army, under number 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if we could then go to Exhibit P 02882.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry. Exhibit P 02882.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Ibrisimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I should like to say that we have spent much more time on the document which Mr. Scott just showed to the witness where the witness was not present, in fact, but we have events where the witness was present and actually signed the document, and as this is about my client, Mr. Pusic, I think it would be in order to actually read out who was attending the meeting, but Mr. Scott is simply skipping over that particular fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The witness has signed, and we have even discussed the signature issue on the last page. I do not quite understand your question, Mr. Ibrisimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I wish the witness to explain who was also representing HVO at this meeting, who else was also representing HVO at this meeting. And the BH army as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir -- sir, you've heard the comment that was made. If you can provide any additional assistance as to who attended the meeting on the 25th of May on the HVO side other than Mr. Puljic and Mr. Maric, if you know.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: I said a while ago there were these two, and apart from them there was all of the military leadership. There was the Jadran Topic, and Berto Pusic, and Petar Zelenika, and many other people came and asked and inquired about what was going on, what the people there were doing. I cannot recall all the names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're saying that on the 25th of May, in addition to those on the list - you are under number 2 - you're saying that there were several other individuals, including Mr. Pusic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So why isn't Mr. Pusic's name on the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know that. He was their chief. I don't know why they signed the document and why he didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Generally speaking, a chief, a head, signs documents. So how would you explain the fact that this document hasn't been signed by him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well -- well, I really don't know. We did know, however, that Berto was the be-all and end-all for all prisoners in the territory in Mostar. He was the one who captured people, who released people. He did so for money. I can tell you that we had information about Kovacevic's mother to that effect. He was working I don't know according to whose orders, probably from on high, but I can tell you, for instance, that in 1992, at Dzemal Bijedic University, the military police set up an investigating prison and they maltreated people there from 1992, 1993, including Serbs; everybody who was against the HZ HB. So if one wanted someone liberated, released, you had to go and talk to Berto Pusic. We do not skirt that issue because that is the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: To get back to the document itself, was this document written and signed on the same day the negotiations were held and concluded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as far as I can recall, this is the way it was done, because when this first document was drawn up on this -- at this first meeting on the 25th, we all placed our signatures on it in the presence of the international community, and of course we could not attend a single meeting without the international community attending. It was impossible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I don't know if it's still been pulled up or not, but if we could go to Exhibit P 02882. Perhaps that's what's on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you see that? Sir, if you can see that document, and again, if you need to see more of it, the registry can assist you by scrolling through the document, but looking at this document, can you tell the Judges what it is.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: That is a work report of our Commission for the Liberation and Exchange of Civilians and Soldiers for the period from the 21st of May to the 21st of June. For a month, in other words. What information we had collected we had translated into this report, and that is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, sir, could you look -- with the assistance of the usher, if they can take us to the last page of that document, which is ERN 03495743. Can you just confirm, Mr. Cupina, that that is your signature, that you signed this document?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: Yes, this is my signature on this document, and also the signature of Amer Bilalovic, who was currently employed with the Ministry of the Interior, in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So, sir, is it correct, then, this is a report that you prepared and signed, or was prepared at your direction?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: That is a report of our commission and the commission had a number of people who all helped draw up the report. I've already listed the names and surnames of the people who were involved in the exchanges. I believe I failed to mention -- I omitted to mention Mr. Buljko, the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see that next to your signature, to the left, it says "Approved by Amer Bilalovic." Who is this person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is a security officer of the 41st Motorised Brigade of the 4th Corps. But as we were friends, we had him also sign the document to the effect that he had received one. That's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll have a break now and that will give everyone enough time to read through this document. It's 20 to 6.00 and we will resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, we have another hour until we adjourn. It would be good if you could conclude your examination-in-chief today so that the Defence can cross-examine the witness tomorrow. You have taken an hour and eight minutes up until now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'll see what I can do, Your Honour. I did -- yes. It's been just a little over an hour, believe it or not, in the actual time that I've taken myself at this juncture, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall a meeting in connection with your work on behalf of the Commission for Exchanges? Do you recall a meeting on the 27th of May, 1993, involving UNHCR?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: Are you referring to this humanitarian meeting with the Commission for Humanitarian Aid and Social Protection?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If that's the meeting you recall, sir. I'm -- just do you recall a meeting on the 27th of May, 1993, involving UNHCR?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And do you recall who else -- was anyone there on behalf of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: I couldn't really say with regard to that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In a report or other documents that we may see today or the Judges may see in this case, there is sometimes reference to an exchange being on the basis of "all for all." Now, that may seem obvious at some level but can you tell the Judges, in connection with an exchange, what does it mean, "all for all"?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: In the document that we signed, representatives of the international community were also present and all members of the military, all civilians, in zones of both entities, and it was said that they had to be released unconditionally in the territory where they lived and worked. It was said that all the civilians and all the members of the military had to be released unconditionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's -- okay. All persons on one side. But how about the exchange on the other side? Again, please listen to my question: What is an "all for all" exchange?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: It means if the ABiH has soldiers or civilians who have been arrested, they have to release them, and similarly, the HVO has to act in this way. However, we always implemented what was on paper. However, the HVO never provided us with a single document, nothing about any detainees, nothing about anyone killed or expelled. They didn't allow us access to concentration camps. They obstructed access and wouldn't cooperate with us. Everything's just orally transmitted. We never received anything on paper from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Before we go forward, can you give the Judges again in the exchange -- in the area of activity of exchanges, what would be a different model. If not all for all, what other kinds of exchanges were there at this time?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: Apart from such exchanges, our commission didn't forbid such exchanges. There were exchanges of individuals. Individuals were involved in that. Our commission was never involved in such exchanges. But as I have already said, according to our information, Berto Pusic was the main person responsible for such exchanges. Whenever it was necessary to exchange somebody for money, for gold, for real estate, et cetera, in many cases such people got involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: The witness is simply not answering the question. Would Mr. Scott please control the witness and ask him to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, please provide a precise answer to the question put to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, can you share with the Judges any observations that you care to make about the conduct of the HVO in connection with exchanges and releases during your dealing, during the time that you were dealing with them on these topics?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: First of all, we compiled a list of soldiers who'd remained at HVO positions. We compiled this list on the basis of information from the parents of soldiers because the documents on the soldiers remained in the territory of responsibility of the HVO. Then we compiled a list of individuals who had been expelled, of children and parents who had been expelled to concentration camps, and then we had lists on those who were in hospitals. However, we never received any such documents from the other side, from the HVO. We never received a single such document. They only listened to what we had to say and then acted in a very arrogant, impudent way. They did everything so that the exchange couldn't take place on the principle all for all that had been agreed on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In connection with exchanges or releases, sir, can you tell the Judges to where or to what locations, in your experience, would prisoners and persons that had been detained, where would they be released to?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: Refugees, people who had been expelled, who had been sent to concentration camps from the -- well, they'd be held at the Heliodrom, Dretelj, the Velez stadium, Dzemal Bijedic University. That's where they would detain them. We never knew how many of them they had released. We received partial information, incomplete information from various individuals. We never had complete information. However, when people crossed over to our side, they would make statements about the terrible torture they'd been subjected to by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Do you know whether some people were released to Croatia or to other countries? If you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm going to object on the leading nature. I understand the gentleman is having a problem with the witness - excuse me, sir - but Mr. Scott should not be leading. This is critical information.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'll restate my question to you. Please listen very carefully to my question. When persons were released or exchanged and they came out of the custody of the other side, from the HVO in particular, do you know where their people were sent, where -- to where, what locations they were released to?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: People were sent to positions near the Hit, near the Bristol Hotel, and then towards Tekija, near Donja Mahala. That's where they sent some people, usually elderly people, women and children. They wanted to burden the ABiH in this way. Some people were sent to other countries, abroad. Some people were converted to a different faith. I've written about this in my book. And I explained in my book that in 1994 that Bishop Peric wrote a letter to Jadranko Prlic and asked him to stop converting Muslims to the Christian faith. We had a list of 159 individuals who were concerned. Unheard of things were done. I couldn't describe such things in one sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. The witness gave a statement about his work from the 24th of May to the 21st of June. We have read through the report that we hadn't read previously. The witness hasn't said anything about this period. Could we establish whether he knows anything about this because of the work he was involved in, or is this all hearsay information and pure speculation?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, a moment ago you said that some were sent abroad. Can you tell us what you know about that.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: Many people were sent abroad. Many people were forced to go abroad. Many wanted to cross over to the left bank, but to do so they had to write over their property to members of the HVO. My own sister Merima Maslo is an exemplary case. She had a child -- children 6 and 9 years old, and she had to go from Mostar to Citluk and try some -- to find an exit of some kind. If friends from Croatia hadn't come to collect her, she would never have managed to reach another country. My brother Mirad was in Tumur [phoen]. He was held there for a month. I'm talking about my family and what they experienced. He ended up in the Gasevci camp. I can provide you with many other examples.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Where was the Gasevci camp, if I heard you correctly? Where was that camp located?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: It was located in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did he remain at that location or did he go somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: The International Red Cross provided him with the paperwork he needed to go to Switzerland, and he now lives there in Singal [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you provide the Judges any information on how it was determined which people would be released to Croatia or third countries and which ones would not?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: They had rules of their own. It depended on the position of the prisoner, on his position in the social hierarchy. That's how they decided. Not a single member of the military, not a single adult was allowed to go to the ABiH or, rather, to the left rank of the Neretva. Only women and children were allowed to do so. These other individuals were selected on the basis of their statements or, rather, on the basis of whether they would provide them with their house, flat, money, et cetera. So that's how they would select them and then send them to third countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When you said just now on the basis of their statements, and you went on it say "or, rather," and I don't know whether you were adding something or correcting that. When you said "on the basis of their statements," what did you mean?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: Yes. There were statements that they gave.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Such as?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: Well, statements according to which they would sign over their property, their flat to someone else. That's the information we received, and we forwarded all the documents on such events to the Ministry of the Interior who was responsible for gathering such information. As far as I know, at the time the chief of the MUP in Mostar was Ramo Maslesa. And this was provided to Alija's institutions in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask the registry to please show you Exhibit P 02884.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: In the meantime, I would like to go back to the lists. The witness has spoken of the lists that they established on the basis of information from parents and others, and I suppose these are lists of people who you supposed were held by the HVO. Did you also provide lists of the people who were held on your side, and did the HVO not present lists of people either they held or people they suspected you held? I hope I made myself clear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as far as the ABiH is concerned at the time, as far as I knew, no one was detained. No civilians or other people. Croats who lived on left bank can confirm this. As far as the right bank is concerned in the HVO's zone of responsibility, this is how we compiled those lists, but they never allowed us to see the people they had. We couldn't check or when they released them -- released them from concentration camps and under what conditions. For a very long time I don't think they even allowed the international community to have access to such information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Would it then be correct to say that if you did not hold any person detained, there could be no question of any exchange?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We discussed the subject of exchanges, and they then compiled a list. I don't know how many people were included. And all those who said they wanted to cross over from the left to the right bank were given the possibility of doing so. All those who wanted to live in Bosnia and Herzegovina, in any part of Bosnia-Herzegovina could do so. The HVO wouldn't allow people to choose the part of Bosnia and Herzegovina they wanted to live in or the territory they wanted to live in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps you could inquire from the witness how is it then earlier he said that the ABiH always complied, meaning that they were exchanging whatever prisoners they had, although now he's saying they never had any, while the HVO wasn't. It just seems to me to be illogical, but maybe in the gentleman's mind there's some, you know, information that he's not telling us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I -- can I try to -- sorry, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Please. Primarily you are questioning the witness. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me try to see if I can help the confusion on this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you've heard the comments in the last few minutes. Perhaps you misunderstood, whatever. There were times when there were exchanges between people that were held on the ABiH side and people that were held on the HVO side; is that correct? There were some exchanges?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: There were exchanges, but as far as I know, they were looking for two soldiers or some soldiers, but as far as I know they were not officially soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Are you saying -- when you go back, and we may be about to lose it -- I guess we already have lost it -- hold on a moment. Sir, you don't have this on your screen any more, but on page 90, line 5, starting at line 5, you were talking about this: "Your Honour, as far as the ABiH is concerned at the time, as far as I know, no one was detained, no civilians or other people. Croats who lived on the left bank can confirm this." You were talking at the time about Croats on the left bank. Are you -- were you -- are you talking there about whether Croats who still lived on the east side had been taken and been detained and kept in custody?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I object to the form of the question. He can ask to clarify his answer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, the -- this idea that questions must not be in any way leading is a rule which in American law of evidence may exist. I wonder where you take any such rule in our Statute or in our Rules of Procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
