utterances.text: Well, I'm glad you mentioned this, because this is the second time you keep pointing to the American system, and I wish to remind the Trial Chamber that when -- when a party calls a witness, it is the witness that needs to testify. By asking a leading question, a leading question suggests the answer, so therefore it is the lawyer that is -- that is providing the information rather than the witness, and to have the Prosecutor now coach the witness with what he might have meant in that instance, we're not getting what the witness might have but, rather, we're getting what the Prosecution is suggesting. And so what I'm asking is a party, whether it's the Prosecution or the Defence, when they call a witness, they should elicit information from the witness. Cross-examination, it's a different technique. But on direct it should be the witness that is should be testifying. And if there's an unclear answer from the witness, the witness should be asked to clarify it by asking him simply could you please tell us who, what, where, why, how, rather than suggesting to the witness what the answer might be. That's because otherwise, when we get back to the record, which you're going to have to use to establish, you know, findings of facts, you are not going to be able to know whether it was the witness's information or whether it was information imparted by the party to the witness. That's why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, you're quite right, but contrary to what takes place in the USA or common law countries, the Judges will read what the question is and will see what the answer is. If the question is leading, the question put by the Prosecution is leading, we'll see what should be done. So rest reassured. However, you are quite right in saying that the Prosecution should not suggest answers to the witness. So the Prosecution has to be careful. However, sometimes the Prosecution tries not to waste time, therefore suggests certain things, and that's a risk one takes. However, the answer shouldn't be provoked by the question when cross -- when examination-in-chief is being conducted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I might ask that -- add, sorry, I also agree in principle. We have had no "Do you still beat your wife?" type questions here. That's the one that really is bad. What happens, if you look at the transcript, is that we have a countless number of interventions of you where you take up an issue with the Prosecutor, who then, after a couple of lost minutes, asks the same question in a slightly different way. It makes practically no difference, and all that happens is that we lose an amazing amount of time by this. When a question is abusively leading, then that's a different matter, but I can hardly remember one like that. And now and then, as the President has said, it's kind of a shortcut that is made here, and we have to go easy about it. This is not a pedagogical exercise where someone must be taught how to do it exactly. The essence is that the truth can come forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I be heard very briefly on that, because evidence is one of the few things in life that I have some claim to know a little about. Your Honour, I have also, like Mr. Karnavas, I think, been a little disturbed by references from the Bench to practice in America. In fact, as the President said, some restraint on the mode of direct examination is common throughout all common law adversarial systems, and Your Honour, with all due respect, trials in this -- in this Tribunal are in fact adversarial proceedings, and the importance of that is that when we -- we are not joining with the Prosecution in a coordinated presentation, as is the system in the civil law countries where everybody knows what the totality of the evidence is before we begin and all that's needed is clarification. What's happening here is that two adversarial parties are presenting their cases. And although Your Honour is quite right in saying there's nothing in the Rules that requires the absence of leading questions, in fact there is a Rule that requires the -- the Trial Chamber - this is Rule 90(F) - to exercise control over the mode and order of interrogating witnesses and presenting evidence so as to make the interrogation and presentation effective for the ascertainment of the truth. Now, I know that sometimes the view is taken that the distinction between common law and civil law that the civil law is more oriented to the ascertainment of the truth, but it's our humble submission as common lawyers that that is our goal also. We may do it in a different way, and our experience suggests that when the Prosecutor can effectively testify for the witness by asking leading questions, it becomes difficult then distinguish what is the Prosecutor's testimony and which is the witness's, and that does not aid the ascertainment of truth. So, Your Honour, there is, in my respectful submission, a certain practical wisdom in exercising a limited mode of control over the examination. I'm not suggesting that we try these proceedings on common law rules of evidence, simply that there should be some limited control in the interests of efficiency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: The controversy is certainly not very deep, and I will leave it at that because otherwise this becomes a seminar, and that is again a loss of time I would be responsible for. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, try to make up for lost time. But at the same time, you should avoid asking leading questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Cupina, I'm going to try to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Scott, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm going to ask this one more time because I think there is perhaps some confusion in the courtroom, or a reasonable question, I'll give you one more chance to answer the question and I'll give up and perhaps the Judges or others will want to follow on. You've told us several times now that there were exchanges between people held which the ABiH and people held by the HVO. I think the question that people are asking in the courtroom is how can people be exchanged unless both sides are holding people? Do you understand the dilemma?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So what people, if any, were the -- was the ABiH side holding that were used for the purposes of conducting exchanges or used that were involved in exchanges?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: The gentleman from the HVO provided a list of people who had to be transferred by us from the left to the right bank.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what about the people that were released or exchanged by the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: I was referring to these individuals who moved around freely in the town, and the army then handed them over and they went to the HVO positions, with the exception of Igor Kapor, who was a problem when an exchange was to be organised because he was a Croatian soldier and the documents about him show that he was a Croatian soldier. They also asked Suad Nametak, an ABiH soldier, to cross over to his -- to their side, and for that reason the exchange was cancelled at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you, sir, to look -- or to be shown Exhibit P 02884. If you can see enough of that document to tell us, sir - and if you can't, we'll try to show more of it to you - can you tell the Judges what that document is?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: This is a report on the work of the Commission for Social Protection and Humanitarian Aid for the period from the 21st of May, to the 21st of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And are you familiar with that report? Have you seen it before today?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: Well, yes. I have it in my archive as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What was the work of this other commission that was going on parallel to the work of the commission that you were also involved in?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: We were in the same premises, the same offices, and this was our joint work, more or less, related to social welfare and protection and humanitarian aid, and just like Mr. Pavlovic says here, that was what we did and I was in contact with him all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now can you tell the Judges, was there a time in connection with this exchange work in which you provided some video material, a video to the HVO?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: I think that Television Croatia made a video of our soldiers of the 4th Corps and the 1st Mostar Brigade who had been captured, and it was in the Vranica building. And the parents would ask us every day about this, because somebody brought in the video, I don't know who, and we handed the video over to the representatives of the international community, and I think the Red Cross as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you provide a copy of the video to anyone connected with the HVO?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: As far as I remember, that copy was handed over to the HVO representatives, but they all said they had nothing to do with it. We never actually received any information about those people during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you recall the particular individual or individuals on the HVO side to whom the video was handed or given?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: As far as I remember, we gave it to the commission, the negotiating commission and the representatives there, because I had nobody else to talk to. It was the negotiating commission which sent it on further, upwards to their superiors.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And do you recall, sir, during this time in negotiations, the individuals on the HVO side that you were dealing with on a regular basis?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: There was Maric, Puljic. They would have contacts with us. Pero Zelenika, Jadran Topic, Berto -- Brko Pusic, rather. I think there was Lugonja, Dr. Lugonja. A series of people. I can't remember all their names just now, but I know that it was jam packed with people. Everybody came to these meetings, everybody who was anybody in Mostar, who occupied HVO posts or HZ HB posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me next direct your attention to Exhibit P 02897. Perhaps that could be enlarged a bit. Thank you. Sir, can you look at that document and can you recognise it; and if so, tell the Judges what it is.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: Yes. This is a document which says that accommodation should be found for displaced persons from the following municipalities: Nevesinje, Gacko, Bileca, and other areas. And that was the area under the occupation -- under the Serbian occupation, occupation by the Serbian army. And we wanted to put these people up before they could go home, so accommodation for the displaced persons and refugees, as well as providing food, shelter, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And looking at the document, sir, can you tell us whether you signed the document? It may need --

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: Yes. I signed that document, as far as I remember, and I made a proposal as to how all those displaced persons could be put up throughout the territory of Mostar municipality so that all the local communes be represented or, rather, that people be put up in facilities in all the local communes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you make this proposal to the HVO?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: Well, I did put forward that proposal. However, they rejected it straight off because they did not want the balijas, as they called them, on their territory, to have balijas on their territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just so the record is clear, maybe it is to most, but when you said in your previous answer "so that all the local communes be represented" - and perhaps it's a translation issue - what do you mean by "local communes"?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: Well, in that area, the ones I mentioned. There were facilities capable of providing accommodation to these people. There was a nursery school. There was -- there were various facilities. Usually nurseries, kindergartens, and so on, that could be adapted to accommodate the people coming in. That's what I mean. There was a hotel as well, Sokol, and a student hostel. Things like that. Buildings and facilities where the displaced persons and refugees could be put up for brief periods of time and could be adapted in a short space of time as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell the Judges the approximate date that you ceased being involved officially as the head of the Exchange Commission on the ABiH side.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: Well, that was when they asked us to go for the exchange to Jablanica, across Dreznica, the new road made by the HVO for its own purposes. Sometime towards the end of 1992 and beginning of 1993. And I ceased to be a member because I didn't feel safe on that territory. And the Spanish Battalion, at a few meetings, was driving an APC to prevent us from being targeted by any of the groups and the RPGs, or whatever the weapons were called. And I think that the representatives of the international community would be able to tell you when that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, you said just now -- you said sometime toward the end of 1992 and beginning of 1993. Sir, we know that you weren't put on the commission until May, 1993. So perhaps there is some confusion about dates. If you could assist us.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: No. I'm referring to the road that was constructed, just the road, when the road was built. The road -- it's a byroad from Djubrani and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm going to come back to my question, sir: Approximately how long did you serve on the commission, then, if you can't remember the exact date? What was the approximate time you served on the commission?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: Well, I was there until I took up my new duties in the Energopetrol company.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And that was that, sir?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: I think up until July, thereabouts. I have the exact date in my documents, but that would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell the Judges, who took your position when you left?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: July of what year, please, so that we have no --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And who took your position or who was named in your place, sir, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: I think it was Alica Alikadic Fakun [phoen], who is no longer in our midst. He's not living any more, not alive any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You continued to live in Mostar, did you, throughout the summer of 1993?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Judges what the conditions in Mostar were at that time as you experienced them? We're now talking about the period roughly May through September, 1993, if you can.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: At that time, the town of Mostar didn't have a single roof left standing. Then there was no water, no electricity, no humanitarian aid coming in, no medicines. There was nothing that a normal livelihood would require. We spent the whole time in caves. We drank water from the river Neretva, which was pumped into a cistern. And from Hum and Planinica you could see where the people were gathering so they could be targeted with heavy artillery. It was -- the conditions were inhumane. Very difficult living conditions, the kind of conditions that do not befit human dignity, but people managed survive without food, without water, without electricity. All they had was what they happened to have in their homes, but otherwise life was very difficult. There was a great deal of illness. Children were exposed to shelling. Old women were shot at by snipers. Genocide was conducted along the demarcation lines. People would lose their lives. They would make them cross over to our side and then shoot them with snipers. It was a terrible time. The situation was very, very difficult, particularly because the displaced persons and refugees were forced to move into our -- in our direction, onto our side. But nobody had any food to eat. The civilians didn't, the soldiers didn't, and when the displaced persons and refugees arrived, the situation was aggravated.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, before we move further, a moment ago you said that water was pumped into a cistern. Just so the record is clear, when you say "cistern," what do you mean? Do you mean a reservoir in the ground, do you mean a well, do you mean a tank? What are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: As far as I remember, it was a fire department's water truck which was used to put out the fires, and the fire brigade was on the left bank. So there was this one water truck that was used which was pumped by generators out of the Neretva River and then supplied to the people. But it's industrial water that you get from the river Neretva, not actually drinking water.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges, please, anything that you observed in connection with the shelling of mosques or other Islamic cultural property in East Mostar -- or East or West Mostar.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: Well, I was witness to many shellings. I saw many of the shellings. It was if they were playing a game to see who would hit a religious -- Muslim site better. Next to my brother's office, for example, at Cernica. All the mosques in the old town. And I also witnessed Biscevic's house, which is a historical monument. So everything that was Islamic was targeted and destroyed. What the Serb and Montenegrin forces failed to do was accomplished by the HVO forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In connection with the -- you mentioned shelling during water -- when water was being collected by the people of East Mostar.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: Well, it was like this: As water -- water was distributed once a day, and since from Planinica or the northern hills above the town you could see all the movement in town, you had to find a safe place, and we changed locations where water would be given out. But whenever they saw the water truck move, they started shelling, and this shelling took place many times. My wife and children were faced with a situation like that, just like all the other citizens of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Apart from shelling, if I can distinguish for a moment sniping, can you tell the Judges a bit more about what you observed in connection with sniping and any experiences that you had personally.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: The sniper fire -- there was sniper fire throughout the war, from Bakina Luka, which is the entrance into Mostar from the north side, to separate the farming area from the town. Then the Buna farming area, to set that apart from Rodoca, and then in the town itself there were large and small calibre snipers from the Catholic church position, then the gymnasium, the Aleksa Santic secondary school, and from the commercial bank, the PBS Bank, or commercial bank building, from there. Then the old people's home was used -- or, rather, opposite the old people's home. There were these high-rise buildings in number 2 Centar where large calibre snipers were used, and I can say that many well-known people died from this sniper fire. During that period of time, for instance, Dr. Pavlovic was killed, and a cousin of mine, Suad Puzic, was killed. Many people lost their lives having been hit by a sniper. And all those records are in the Ministry of the Interior. It was all recorded, and I think that that is material that is accessible to people who want to have exact facts and figures about all this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Sorry. What do you understand to be a large calibre, and how do you know whether it was a large calibre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, because they were PATs and PAMs, the calibres; PATs and PAMs. They had optic sights, special optic sights. Anti-aircraft machine-guns and cannons. And I was with Goran Fink. His wife was about to give birth, and he said we should go and find some milk. We went to the marketplace, and he was hit, most probably, according to our information, from a position up on the high-rise building, a long way away, by the Catholic church. A sniper hit him. And it's a long distance. So that's why. As the crow flies, it's a very long time, that is to say the distance between the sniper's nest and where the person was hit, right behind the Catholic church, which means you have to cross the Neretva River and then it's 3 or 400 metres at least away from that. That's where that sniper position was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, with the usher's assistance I would like to show you in hard copy, and it can be placed on the ELMO, a copy of P 09517. Sir, in preparing to give your testimony today, were you shown a map and asked to make certain -- to mark certain locations on the map? And what's on the ELMO now, do you notice -- do you recognise that to be the paper on which you made your markings?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I direct your attention first of all to the marking number 1, that is the number 1. Can you tell us what is marked -- what you intended to mark or signify by marking that location.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: That is the position of the mosque at the beginning of Cernica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what can you tell us about that mosque? What did you see or know about the condition --

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: It is one of the oldest mosques in Mostar which was shelled by the HVO, and it was destroyed. It was hit -- targeted, hit and destroyed. After the war, it was reconstructed, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Does the witness have an idea as to when it was shelled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All the mosques -- well, all the mosques were targeted from May and June throughout - I can't remember the exact date - until they were ultimately destroyed, but my brother's office, who is a lawyer, is nearby. It's near that mosque, so I had occasion to see that happening because I was looking for documents relating to some property that I had, a house I had, and so on. So I spent a lot of time there, searching for those documents, and I could see that happening, and I was in that area, Cernica, fairly frequently during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So that the record is clear, sir, when you say May and June, what year are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, quickly, Mr. Kovacic. It's already five to 7.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I hate to interrupt, but according to the way in which we produce evidence, I think following your guidelines, you -- we used to ask that the witness makes his markings in the courtroom. It seems that he marked this before, made the markings before and just confirmed them here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Scott. I understood the witness to have marked these things previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's correct. Just as we've done with other witnesses who have done the same thing, with no objection from the Court, ahead of time. It simply saves time in the courtroom, Your Honour. The witness can make the markings. He's subject to full cross-examination on the map. It takes a lot less time to do it outside the courtroom than inside the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll go on to number 2 and 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, what's at location number 2?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: The mosque is at the bottom and it's still in Cernica. It's the local commune of Cernica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What happened to the mosque at that location?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: It was shelled continuously, and my friend Mirza Hadziomerovic was nearby there, he lived nearby, and we would watch the shelling of the mosque and then take shelter. They destroyed it in stages, but mostly all the mosques were half destroyed, 50 per cent destroyed, and some of them were razed to the ground as well. I didn't carry out an exact appraisal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you say "he," who was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "They." When you say "they," who do you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mean the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir -- Your Honour, I think we'll need a few minutes in the morning, not very long, but if I could just finish with number 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, when you made the marking at number 3, what's at that location -- or was at that location?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: That's also a mosque, one of the most famous mosques, Karadzoz-bey mosque in Fejica Street. It's the oldest mosque and a symbol of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What happened to that mosque, please?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: It was also destroyed, although it was -- and all these mosques were under the protection of the Cultural Institute of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So that one was destroyed too. It was targeted by the HVO units.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I'll need about 15 minutes tomorrow to finish. We're almost at the end, but I'll need a few minutes in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we could ask him what A, B, C, D denotes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I was going to do that in the morning, but if Your Honour wants to continue, I'm happy to continue now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if you still have that available to you, then, can you tell us what is indicated by the location marked as A?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: A is the secondary school, the Aleksa Santic secondary school. But these were the fascist names of streets, because it did not exist before the war, that was still present in Mostar. Those are the streets and this is a new map, which is inappropriate to a civilised Europe. A is the gymnasium or the secondary school; B is the glass building; C is the Bristol Hotel; D is the old people's home, retirement home. So A, B -- D. Yes, those were snipers' nests that covered all the bridges over the Neretva River, so it was impossible to cross from one bank to the other. That would be it, roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm just looking at my notes and you did at that rather quick. Let me -- okay. I think we're up to A, B, C and D. Can you tell us what is indicated by location E?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: The letter E denotes the Catholic church and the position of the high-rise building. I think there were two tall blocks there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did you mark this -- have you marked that again as a -- what you identified as a sniping position, sniper position?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: Yes, they were sniper positions. On the left bank -- let's see how far that is, what the distance is. Goran Fink was hit across the Neretva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me just ask you: What is indicated at location G?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't get the translation. The witness said something just now.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: G is Bakina Luka, a residential building, which is where there was a sniper's nest which covered the entrance to Mostar in order to separate the town of Mostar from the farming or -- farming zone. That is to say, to separate supplies from coming in. It's the M17 motorway, or road, which was the entrance into Mostar from the Bijelo Polje direction. The H is the sniper nest. It's a hill, Stotina. There are a few houses there which covered -- and from there they covered Hasan Brkic bridge. And G is the position of the residential buildings. It's an agrarian area, a farming area, once again to cut off the supply route.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: G or J?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: That's the G, yes, Rodoc.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What looks to me on the map -- are you talking about the marking that's immediately above the word "Rodoc"?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: Rodoc, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you consider that, sir, just so the record is clear, do you consider that to be a G or a J? Maybe it's a translation --

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: J, yes, J.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you. I think the only one we may have missed, sir, is F. I didn't -- I'm not sure I heard you say -- if you can find location F on the map, please.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: Yes. That's the centre, the central or local commune, with a number of high-rise buildings from which they were able to cover the area towards Carina, the entrance into Mostar town. There's Severni, North Camp, and Gavro's house next to the Carina bridge. And further on towards Zalik, a residential district called Zalik. And the 100 -- or, rather, Stotina was a sniper nest, and they had tanks there too, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. I'm --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to conclude, but before we do, just let me clarify the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, again, just so the record is clear because sometimes the markings, at least on the ELMO, may not look entirely clear, when you referred to -- let's see, F, were you referring to what's -- the marking that's under a location marked Centar II?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Your Honour -- Your Honour, I appreciate the Court's patience, but I still think there will be a few wrap-up questions and I'll need just a few minutes in the morning, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just before we close, a moment ago, when you referred to A, you said the secondary school, or gymnasium, which was destroyed by the fascists, and I saw Mr. Praljak jumping up. What allows you to say that they were fascists? What makes you say that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as far as I'm concerned, everything that is inhumane and contrary to civilised behaviour - persecution, ethnic cleansing, the killing of small children, parents, elderly persons - every -- all that, because people have different ideas. So everything that builds up civilisation. And it was the stifling of civilisation in the Mostar region. That I refer to as fascism. And that is why these streets were named taking the names of the soldiers of the NDH, the Independent State of Croatia, who were on the side of the fascist movement. So that the cultural centre, for example, changed its name. It was built by Mostar citizens. It was called the Kosaca centre, for example. Then the Velez football stadium was called the Zrinski. So that's still happening today. All the street names are being changed to take the names of people who had been condemned as fascists after World War II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quickly, Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm not used to being insulted. I've been brought here, or I came here voluntarily, to determine what I'm guilty of. Witnesses appear here to say when, what, where, how. If witnesses are allowed to call entire people fascists, to talk about the Kings of Kosaca from the 14th or 15th century in such a way, to call them such names, then this becomes a political pamphlet, political pamphleteering, hurling insults, and this is not the appropriate place to act in such a manner. I would be grateful if we could adhere to the Rules and if witnesses could act correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's why I wanted to ask whether this was a personal opinion of yours. Yes. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think it would be helpful if we read out the names of the streets under A and B. It's not very clear here. The streets are called Kolodvorska, Aleksa Santica Street, and then there is a street called something like Zelena Ulice [phoen]. These names have absolutely nothing to do with the names of soldiers, least of all the names of soldiers from the NDH who died in the case -- in the cause of the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll deal with this perhaps tomorrow, but the issue of names has already been dealt with. This was done when you weren't present and when we had another witness testifying here. It's now ten past 7.00. I apologise to the interpreters, and we will meet again tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 11th day of July, 2006, at 9.00 a.m. 25
